title: The DEC PDP-11 I: Minicomputers, the UNIBUS & 16-Bit Architecture (1957–1975)
summary: Part 1 of the DEC PDP-11 series: a relaxed, generalist-friendly 100-question journey from 1950s batch-processing mainframes, DEC's Maynard woolen mill, and the 12-bit PDP-8 to the 1970 unveiling of the 16-bit PDP-11/20. With zero assumed computer-architecture jargon, learners unpack little-endian bytes, the asynchronous UNIBUS, memory-mapped I/O, general-purpose registers R0–R7, orthogonal auto-increment instructions, magnetic core memory, RK05 disk packs, octal front-panel bootstrapping, and the PDP-11/45 and 11/70 Memory Management Units—setting the stage for the software and Unix revolution of Part II.
topic_prompt: Teach Part 1 of a 2-part series on the history and architecture of DEC's PDP-11 for an educated generalist with zero assumed computer-architecture jargon. Begin with the computing landscape of the late 1950s and 1960s: IBM's closed-door batch-processing mainframes versus Ken Olsen and Harlan Anderson founding Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) inside a Civil War-era woolen mill in Maynard, Massachusetts, championing affordable, interactive 'hands-on' minicomputers (PDP-1 and the 12-bit PDP-8). Explain why 12-bit words and single-accumulator designs hit a ceiling as 8-bit ASCII text proliferated, and how the cancelled 'PDP-X' project cleared the way for Gordon Bell, Harold McFarland, Roger Cady, and their team to unveil the 16-bit PDP-11/20 in 1970. Gently unpack each pillar of the PDP-11's architecture using concrete, intuitive analogies: 8-bit bytes inside 16-bit words (a $$2^{16} = 65{,}536$$-byte or 64 KB address space) and 'little-endian' byte ordering; the revolutionary asynchronous UNIBUS where the CPU, core memory, and peripherals communicate as peers on a single shared highway; memory-mapped I/O (controlling teletypes and disk drives simply by reading and writing reserved memory addresses instead of using special I/O instructions); the eight 16-bit general-purpose registers (R0–R7, with R6 as the hardware Stack Pointer and R7 as the Program Counter); and 'orthogonal' instructions paired with auto-increment and auto-decrement addressing modes that made data stacks and position-independent code effortless. Conclude with the tactile experience of magnetic core memory, removable RK05 disk packs, toggling octal boot loaders into a blinking PDP-11 front-panel console, and how the PDP-11/45 and legendary PDP-11/70 used Memory Management Units and split Instruction/Data spaces to expand beyond 64 KB—setting the stage for the operating systems and global software legacy of Part II.

sections.title: 1. Mainframe Priesthoods vs. the Maynard Mill: Birth of the Minicomputer (1957–1965)
sections.summary: Begin in the late 1950s and early 1960s, when computing meant submitting decks of punched cards through a window to an air-conditioned IBM 'glass house' and waiting hours or days for printed results. Follow MIT Lincoln Laboratory engineers Ken Olsen and Harlan Anderson as they establish Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) in 1957 inside a Civil War-era brick woolen mill in Maynard, Massachusetts, progressing from transistorized 'Flip-Chip' lab modules to the interactive 1960 PDP-1 and the cabinet-sized 1965 PDP-8 that put hands-on computing within reach of laboratories and classrooms.

chunks.title: The Glass-House Priesthood of Batch Processing
chunks.content_markdown:
Imagine trying to write an essay if you were forbidden to touch the typewriter. Instead, you had to hand handwritten slips of paper through a slot to a uniformed attendant, wait twenty-four hours, and receive a single sheet reading: 'Punctuation error on line 4; job halted.'

In the late 1950s and early 1960s, that was how nearly all scientific and corporate computing worked. Giant corporate systems like the IBM 7090—known as **batch-processing mainframes**—filled entire raised-floor, air-conditioned rooms behind plate-glass observation windows. Because a single mainframe could cost millions of dollars to buy or tens of thousands of dollars per month to rent, no ordinary engineer or student was allowed near the console.

Instead, users punched their programs onto stacks of stiff paper cards and surrendered the deck at a reception counter. White-coated operators gathered dozens of separate card decks into a single 'batch' so the machine never sat idle while a human thought. If a single card had one mistyped character, you only discovered the mistake the next morning when your paper printout came back.

questions.prompt: Why did 1950s and 1960s mainframe centers group user programs into 'batches' run by dedicated operators rather than letting programmers run jobs directly?
choices: Because early magnetic storage could only read data when dozens of separate programs were merged together
Because astronomical machine rental costs made it too expensive for the processor to sit idle while humans typed
Because federal safety laws barred untrained university researchers from entering high-voltage rooms
Because early punch-card readers physically jammed unless fed several thousand cards in a continuous stream
questions.explanation: Mainframes cost millions of dollars to purchase or tens of thousands per month to rent, so computer centers kept the machine continuously busy by having dedicated operators feed non-stop batches of jobs rather than waiting for an individual human to think or type.

questions.prompt: What was the biggest everyday frustration for a programmer debugging code on a closed-door batch-processing mainframe?
choices: Even a tiny typing error required waiting hours or overnight just to see the failure printout
Every programmer had to rewire the processor's internal circuit boards before submitting a deck
Mainframe printers could only output raw binary ones and zeros rather than readable alphabet letters
Operators routinely erased magnetic memory between lines of code inside the same submitted program
questions.explanation: Because programmers handed their card decks through a counter window and waited for their turn in an operator-run batch queue, discovering and fixing a single syntax mistake could take an entire day.

chunks.title: Whirlwind, TX-0, and the Maynard Woolen Mill
chunks.content_markdown:
A handful of young electrical engineers in Cambridge, Massachusetts, knew computing did not have to feel so distant. At MIT's Lincoln Laboratory, **Ken Olsen** and **Harlan Anderson** helped build experimental machines—first Whirlwind and then the transistorized TX-0—where a single researcher sat directly at a glowing cathode-ray screen, flipped switches, and watched the machine respond in real time.

Convinced that engineers everywhere hungered for that direct, responsive experience, Olsen and Anderson sought funding in 1957 from Georges Doriot's American Research and Development Corporation (ARDC), one of the first modern venture-capital firms. With $$\$70{,}000$$ in seed capital, they founded **Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC)** inside a sprawling, Civil War-era brick woolen mill in Maynard, Massachusetts.

Yet Doriot warned them not to pitch a full computer right away; in 1957, Wall Street believed only giant corporations like IBM could survive in the computer business. So DEC began by selling rugged, plug-in transistor circuit cards—later famous as **Flip-Chip** modules—that laboratory scientists could wire together to test electronics and automate experiments.

questions.prompt: What formative experience at MIT's Lincoln Laboratory inspired Ken Olsen and Harlan Anderson's vision for Digital Equipment Corporation?
choices: Operating massive accounting tabulators that processed millions of census cards without human intervention
Sitting directly at interactive machines like Whirlwind and TX-0 that responded immediately to user controls
Designing transatlantic telegraph repeaters that transmitted five-bit financial ticker codes across Europe
Managing a commercial time-sharing bureau that billed corporate accountants by the millisecond
questions.explanation: At MIT Lincoln Lab, Olsen and Anderson worked on Whirlwind and the transistorized TX-0, where one researcher could interact directly with the machine via switches and a display screen in real time.

questions.prompt: Why did Digital Equipment Corporation initially sell modular transistor circuit boards from its Maynard woolen mill rather than pitching a full computer in 1957?
choices: Transistors had not yet been invented in 1957, forcing DEC to sell vacuum-tube replacement parts first
Patent treaties signed with MIT prohibited DEC from building programmable processors for five years
Investors believed small startups could not compete head-on with giant mainframe makers like IBM
The Maynard woolen mill lacked sufficient electrical wiring to power a complete computer system
questions.explanation: Venture capitalist Georges Doriot advised Olsen and Anderson that investors viewed full computers as a money-losing domain dominated by giants like IBM, so DEC profitably launched by selling modular digital test building blocks first.

chunks.title: Why Call a Computer a 'Programmed Data Processor'?
chunks.content_markdown:
By 1959, DEC engineer Ben Gurley had shown that the company's off-the-shelf transistor modules could be assembled into a complete, interactive machine modeled on MIT's TX-0. When DEC unveiled the machine in 1960, however, Olsen and Anderson carefully avoided calling it a 'computer.'

In corporate and government budgets of 1960, the word 'computer' meant a million-dollar IBM behemoth requiring boardroom approval, a dedicated air-conditioned facility, and a permanent staff of operators. To bypass that bureaucratic wall, DEC christened its machine the **PDP-1**—short for **Programmed Data Processor**.

Priced at $$\$120{,}000$$ (a fraction of a comparable mainframe), the PDP-1 arrived ready to plug into a standard laboratory floor without a glass-walled temple. A researcher could sit at its built-in typewriter console and round cathode-ray screen, load a punched paper tape, and interact with programs live. In 1962, MIT students led by Steve Russell even used a donated PDP-1 to create *Spacewar!*, the first two-player interactive video game—something unimaginable on a batch-processing mainframe.

questions.prompt: Why did DEC name its 1960 system a 'Programmed Data Processor' (PDP-1) instead of calling it a 'computer'?
choices: Because the PDP-1 could only execute permanently wired arithmetic routines and lacked stored-program memory
Because the word 'computer' triggered executive budget reviews associated with million-dollar mainframes
Because IBM held an exclusive federal trademark on the word 'computer' throughout the 1960s
Because the PDP-1 was marketed exclusively to telephone companies as an analog voice switchboard
questions.explanation: In 1960, calling a machine a 'computer' suggested an expensive, operator-staffed mainframe installation; 'Programmed Data Processor' positioned the PDP-1 as practical laboratory equipment that engineering departments could purchase directly.

questions.prompt: What did the creation of the 1962 game Spacewar! on MIT's PDP-1 vividly demonstrate about DEC's design philosophy?
choices: That punched card decks could be sorted twice as fast when operators used round display screens
That commercial arcades had already surpassed scientific laboratories as DEC's primary source of revenue
That vacuum-tube mainframes were better suited to real-time graphics than solid-state transistors
That interactive machines allowed live human control and visual feedback impossible in batch queues
questions.explanation: Spacewar! relied on two humans flipping real-time controls while watching spacecraft move on a live display—showcasing the immediate, hands-on interactivity that set DEC's machines apart from batch mainframes.

chunks.title: The 1965 PDP-8 and the 'Minicomputer' Revolution
chunks.content_markdown:
If the PDP-1 cracked open the door to hands-on computing, the **PDP-8**, designed by Edson de Castro and unveiled in 1965, blew the door off its hinges. Thanks to high-density Flip-Chip modules and automated **wire-wrapped backplanes** (frames of connector pins wired together behind the circuit cards), the base PDP-8 fit inside a tabletop cabinet the size of a dorm refrigerator and cost just $$\$18{,}500$$.

For the first time, a university physics lab, a factory floor, or a hospital clinic could buy a computer outright out of a departmental equipment grant. Paired with a rugged **Teletype Model 33 ASR**—an electromechanical teleprinter with a keyboard, roll printer, and paper-tape punch/reader—the PDP-8 birthed a new category of machine: the **interactive minicomputer**.

Reportedly coined by John Leng, head of DEC's London office, by analogy with Britain's trendy Mini Cooper car and 1960s miniskirt, the name 'minicomputer' captured both its compact size and its approachable spirit. Over $$50{,}000$$ PDP-8 systems were eventually sold, proving that thousands of scientists and engineers wanted a personal, hands-on machine rather than a distant mainframe slice.

questions.prompt: How did the 1965 PDP-8 transform who could own and operate a digital computer?
choices: Its battery-powered briefcase chassis allowed traveling executives to type spreadsheets on commercial flights
Its built-in color television receiver turned it into a mass-market home appliance for suburban families
Its $$\$18{,}500$$ price and tabletop size let individual labs and factories buy a machine without executive approval
Its compatibility with IBM punch-card sorters let banks replace every mainframe operator overnight
questions.explanation: At $$\$18{,}500$$ and roughly the size of a small refrigerator, the PDP-8 was cheap and compact enough for individual research labs, factories, and clinics to buy directly and embed in daily work.

questions.prompt: What everyday peripheral device served as the standard human interface for typing commands and reading output on a typical PDP-8?
choices: An 80-column IBM 029 keypunch machine connected to a high-speed optical card sorter
A Teletype Model 33 ASR teleprinter with a keyboard, paper roll printer, and paper-tape station
A three-button optical mouse paired with a high-resolution bitmapped laser printer
A magnetic-stripe badge reader wired to a wall of electromechanical stock-ticker domes
questions.explanation: The inexpensive Teletype Model 33 ASR combined a keyboard, an impact printer on continuous paper rolls, and a paper-tape reader/punch, making it the classic interactive console for the PDP-8.

chunks.title: Two Worlds of Computing—and a New Growing Pain
chunks.content_markdown:
By the late 1960s, the computing world had split into two distinct cultures. In corporate data centers, **batch-processing mainframes** still ruled payroll, banking, and airline reservations behind glass walls. Meanwhile, in laboratories, universities, and industrial plants, DEC's **Programmed Data Processors** had established the **interactive minicomputer** as a nimble, hands-on tool.

Look at what changed when the glass wall came down:
- **Access:** Instead of handing cards to an operator, you flipped switches and typed on a Teletype yourself.
- **Turnaround:** Instead of waiting overnight to catch a typo, you saw your program's behavior in seconds.
- **Cost & Scale:** Instead of one million-dollar machine shared by a whole corporation, a department owned a compact machine dedicated to its work.

Yet the very success of the PDP-8 soon created a headache for Ken Olsen's engineers in Maynard. Customers were no longer using minicomputers just to count pulses from a single physics detector—they wanted to edit text documents, manage multiple users, and write complex software. And inside the PDP-8, a fundamental hardware limit was about to get in the way.

questions.prompt: Which contrast best summarizes the cultural divide between 1960s IBM mainframes and DEC minicomputers?
choices: Mainframes relied on operator-run batch queues, whereas minicomputers gave users direct interactive control
Mainframes processed only scientific laboratory data, whereas minicomputers handled only corporate payroll
Mainframes used punched paper tape for storage, whereas minicomputers required 80-column card decks
Mainframes were sold exclusively to universities, whereas minicomputers were leased only to federal agencies
questions.explanation: Mainframe culture emphasized centralized, operator-scheduled batch throughput, while DEC's minicomputer culture championed direct, interactive, hands-on access by scientists, engineers, and students.

questions.prompt: Why did the runaway success of the PDP-8 create an urgent architectural challenge for DEC by the late 1960s?
choices: The U.S. government outlawed 12-bit minicomputers in favor of standardized 64-bit supercomputers
Supply shortages of Civil War-era brick space in Maynard forced DEC to abandon hardware manufacturing
Teletype machines stopped supporting binary electrical signals and switched entirely to analog voice audio
Customers began demanding text processing and complex software that strained the PDP-8's simple hardware
questions.explanation: As minicomputers moved beyond simple lab instrumentation into text editing, multi-user systems, and larger programs, users rapidly ran into the internal architectural limits of the PDP-8.

sections.title: 2. The 12-Bit Ceiling, the PDP-X Crisis & the Birth of the PDP-11 (1965–1970)
sections.summary: Build from first principles what a binary bit and a processor's fixed 'word length' mean, exploring why the PDP-8's 12-bit words and single-workbench register ('accumulator') worked brilliantly for simple lab instruments but strained as 8-bit ASCII text characters and larger programs became standard. Trace the internal debates that led Ken Olsen to cancel the ambitious 16-bit 'PDP-X' project, and see how Carnegie Mellon returnee Gordon Bell joined Harold McFarland, Roger Cady, and their engineering team to craft the clean, revolutionary 16-bit PDP-11/20 unveiled in January 1970.

chunks.title: What Is a 'Word' Inside a Computer?
chunks.content_markdown:
To understand why DEC's bestselling PDP-8 ran into trouble in the late 1960s, we first need to unpack two foundational ideas from scratch: a **bit** and a **word**.

At the lowest physical level, a digital circuit is just a switch that is either off ($$0$$) or on ($$1$$). Each individual $$0$$-or-$$1$$ switch is called a **bit** (short for *binary digit*). Because a single bit cannot say much on its own, a computer groups a fixed number of bits together into a standard bundle that its processor fetches, adds, and stores in a single gulp. That natural bundle size is called the machine's **word length**.

The 1965 PDP-8 was built around a **12-bit word length**: every memory slot and arithmetic circuit handled 12 bits at a time, giving $$2^{12} = 4{,}096$$ possible patterns per word. For reading a laboratory voltage sensor or counting radiation clicks, 12 bits was a sweet spot—accurate to one part in $$4{,}096$$, while requiring very few expensive transistor circuits.

questions.prompt: In computer architecture, what does a machine's 'word length' describe?
choices: The maximum number of English letters allowed in a variable name inside a programming language
The physical length in inches of the copper ribbon cable connecting the keyboard to the printer
The standard fixed bundle of binary bits that the processor fetches and manipulates as a single unit
The number of seconds required for the magnetic memory to complete one full startup cycle
questions.explanation: A computer's word length is the fixed number of binary bits (such as 12 bits on the PDP-8 or 16 bits on the PDP-11) that the processor naturally fetches, stores, and calculates with in one operation.

questions.prompt: Why was a 12-bit word length so attractive when DEC designed the original PDP-8 for laboratory instruments in 1965?
choices: It provided 4,096 levels of precision while keeping the number of expensive transistor circuits small
It matched the exact number of decimal digits used in international banking wire transfers
It allowed a single word to store twelve complete English sentences without compression
It guaranteed that the processor would never need more than twelve watts of electrical power
questions.explanation: With $$2^{12} = 4{,}096$$ distinct values, a 12-bit word offered ample precision for laboratory sensors while minimizing the number of costly transistors required in every register and arithmetic circuit.

chunks.title: The 8-Bit ASCII Squeeze and the Lone Workbench
chunks.content_markdown:
Within a few years of 1965, two shifts turned the PDP-8's 12-bit economy into a painful squeeze. First, the computing industry rallied around **ASCII** (the American Standard Code for Information Interchange) to represent text characters, and IBM's landmark System/360 mainframe popularized storing each character inside an **8-bit byte** (a power-of-two chunk of 8 bits).

Try fitting 8-bit character bytes into a 12-bit PDP-8 word! One 8-bit character leaves 4 leftover bits wasted, or forces programmers to write clumsy bit-slicing routines to cram three 8-bit characters across two 12-bit words. Also, a 12-bit address could directly name only $$2^{12} = 4{,}096$$ words of memory, split into tiny 128-word 'pages' that were awkward to cross.

Second, the PDP-8 used a **single-accumulator architecture**. Imagine a carpenter's shop with thousands of storage cubbies on the wall (main memory), but only **one tiny workbench**—called the **accumulator**—where tools can actually touch wood. To add two numbers, the PDP-8 had to clear the workbench, fetch number A, add number B, and immediately pack the result back to a wall cubby before doing anything else.

questions.prompt: Why did the industry-wide rise of 8-bit byte character storage make the PDP-8's 12-bit word length awkward for text processing?
choices: Because a 12-bit word could only hold numbers up to 12, whereas the English alphabet has 26 letters
Because 12 does not divide evenly by 8, forcing programmers to waste bits or split characters across words
Because 8-bit characters required alternating current, while 12-bit processors ran on direct current
Because ASCII text rules prohibited any computer with an even word length from printing lowercase letters
questions.explanation: An 8-bit byte fits cleanly twice inside a 16-bit word, but inside a 12-bit word it either wastes 4 bits per word or requires awkward bit-packing routines to straddle three bytes across two words.

questions.prompt: In the carpenter's workshop analogy, what is the drawback of a 'single-accumulator architecture' like the PDP-8?
choices: The computer can only connect to a single keyboard and must unplug it whenever the printer runs
The arithmetic circuit can only perform addition and must halt whenever subtraction is requested
The memory cabinet can store only one program instruction at a time before erasing itself
The processor has only one internal working register, forcing constant saving and reloading to main memory
questions.explanation: In a single-accumulator machine, almost every calculation flows through one lone working register (the accumulator), so intermediate values must be continually copied back and forth to slower main memory.

chunks.title: Rivals at the Gate and the Cancelled 'PDP-X'
chunks.content_markdown:
By 1967, DEC's rivals had spotted the 12-bit vulnerability. Computer Control Company (soon bought by Honeywell), Hewlett-Packard, and Interdata began shipping **16-bit minicomputers** whose 16-bit words held two 8-bit bytes cleanly side by side. Even worse for DEC, in 1968 the PDP-8's own chief designer, Edson de Castro, left DEC with several colleagues to found **Data General**, launching the fast, inexpensive 16-bit **Nova**.

Inside DEC's Maynard mill, an engineering group had spent nearly two years designing a 16-bit successor code-named **PDP-X**. On paper, PDP-X was a capable 16-bit design, but as committees added features, it grew into a sprawling, expensive family of machines that looked too much like a conventional medium-scale mainframe.

In late 1968, Ken Olsen made the gutsy call to cancel PDP-X outright. Olsen worried that PDP-X was neither cheap enough to beat Data General's Nova nor bold enough in its architecture to define the next decade. Several frustrated PDP-X engineers quit, leaving DEC in an urgent race to invent a true 16-bit breakthrough from a clean sheet of paper.

questions.prompt: What competitive shock in 1968 underscored DEC's urgent need for a modern 16-bit minicomputer?
choices: PDP-8 designer Edson de Castro left DEC to co-found Data General and launch the 16-bit Nova
IBM gave away free System/360 mainframes to every university that agreed to return its PDP-8
Teletype Corporation refused to sell keyboards for any computer with fewer than 16 bits per word
MIT revoked DEC's license to use transistorized Flip-Chip modules in commercial laboratory products
questions.explanation: Along with 16-bit entrants from HP, Honeywell, and Interdata, the departure of PDP-8 architect Edson de Castro to found Data General and build the 16-bit Nova put intense pressure on DEC.

questions.prompt: Why did Ken Olsen cancel DEC's internal 16-bit 'PDP-X' project in late 1968?
choices: He believed that 8-bit ASCII text was a passing fad and wanted DEC to return to 6-bit machines
The PDP-X prototype caught fire in the Maynard mill and destroyed the only set of blueprints
He judged that PDP-X had grown too complex and costly without offering a true architectural leap
Market surveys showed that scientists preferred batch punch-card mainframes over interactive systems
questions.explanation: Olsen feared the committee-driven PDP-X had bloated into an overly complex, expensive design without a sufficiently innovative architecture to set DEC apart from new 16-bit competitors.

chunks.title: Gordon Bell, the Desk Calculator, and the 16-Bit Breakthrough
chunks.content_markdown:
After cancelling PDP-X, DEC formed a small, nimble design group including **Harold McFarland**, **Roger Cady**, **Jim O'Loughlin**, and **Ronnie Noonan**, guided by DEC's brilliant architectural mastermind **Gordon Bell**, who had been teaching computer science at Carnegie Mellon University.

At first, the team explored two tracks: a tiny, ultra-cheap 8-bit 'Desk Calculator' (code-named DCM) and a larger 16-bit machine. Soon they realized that if they designed the 16-bit processor cleanly enough, it could manipulate individual 8-bit bytes just as effortlessly as full 16-bit words—making a separate 8-bit machine unnecessary.

Even more decisive was input from software engineers, including Carnegie Mellon's Bill Wulf and DEC's Larry Portner, who reviewed an early draft of the instruction set. When they pointed out that irregular, special-purpose registers made compilers and operating systems painful to write, Bell and McFarland scrapped the messy draft over a single weekend. In its place, they created a radically symmetrical 16-bit architecture with eight interchangeable registers and a single unified system bus.

questions.prompt: Why did DEC's design team abandon the idea of building a separate 8-bit 'Desk Calculator' alongside their new 16-bit machine?
choices: They discovered that 8-bit circuits consumed four times as much electricity as 16-bit circuits
They designed the 16-bit processor to handle both 8-bit bytes and 16-bit words with equal ease
Federal export regulations prohibited American companies from selling 8-bit calculators overseas
Customers insisted that every number in a laboratory experiment had to be at least five digits long
questions.explanation: By giving their 16-bit architecture native ability to address and manipulate individual 8-bit bytes as well as 16-bit words, one clean architecture covered both small byte-oriented tasks and full 16-bit computing.

questions.prompt: How did feedback from software designers like Bill Wulf reshape the final architecture of the PDP-11?
choices: It convinced DEC to remove all internal registers and run arithmetic directly on paper tape
It led the team to copy the exact 12-bit instruction codes of the PDP-8 so no new manuals were needed
It persuaded Ken Olsen to hard-wire the FORTRAN language permanently into the power supply
It prompted Bell and McFarland to replace irregular special registers with a clean, symmetrical design
questions.explanation: When software reviewers showed how awkward special-case instructions and registers were for writing compilers and system software, Gordon Bell and Harold McFarland redesigned the processor around clean, general-purpose symmetry.

chunks.title: January 1970: Unveiling the PDP-11/20
chunks.content_markdown:
In January 1970, DEC officially unveiled the **PDP-11/20**, the first member of the new 16-bit family. Priced at $$\$10{,}800$$ for a basic processor (or roughly $$\$20{,}000$$ with memory and a console teleprinter), the PDP-11/20 was an instant sensation that eventually grew into a twenty-year line selling hundreds of thousands of units.

What made the PDP-11/20 feel like a breath of fresh air compared to the 12-bit PDP-8 and its 16-bit rivals?
- **Native 8-bit bytes inside 16-bit words:** Every 16-bit word held exactly two 8-bit ASCII characters, and every individual byte had its own memory address.
- **A unified highway (the UNIBUS):** The processor, memory, and input/output devices all plugged into one shared communication bus.
- **Eight general-purpose workbenches:** Instead of a single bottlenecked accumulator, programmers had eight 16-bit registers (`R0`–`R7`) working with a remarkably regular instruction set.

Over the next five sections, we will gently open the hood of the PDP-11 and explore each of these architectural pillars one by one—starting with how bytes and words live inside its 64-kilobyte memory.

questions.prompt: Which combination of breakthroughs set the 1970 PDP-11/20 apart from the earlier 12-bit PDP-8?
choices: Byte-addressable 16-bit words, eight general-purpose registers, and a single shared UNIBUS highway
Vacuum-tube logic modules, a single accumulator register, and an 80-column punch-card console
A 36-bit scientific word length, water-cooled cabinetry, and operator-only batch job scheduling
Three-bit character encoding, dedicated radial I/O cables, and fixed 128-word memory pages
questions.explanation: The PDP-11/20 replaced the PDP-8's 12-bit single-accumulator design with byte-addressable 16-bit words, eight 16-bit general-purpose registers, and the unified UNIBUS.

questions.prompt: Why was moving from a 12-bit word to a byte-addressable 16-bit word on the PDP-11/20 such a relief for programmers working with text?
choices: A 16-bit word allowed the processor to store sixteen full pages of English prose inside one register
Byte addressing eliminated the need for main memory by storing all documents inside the keyboard cable
Each 16-bit word held two 8-bit ASCII characters cleanly, and every single byte had its own address
Sixteen-bit words automatically translated English sentences into French and German without software
questions.explanation: Because $$16 = 2 \times 8$$, a 16-bit word holds two 8-bit ASCII characters without leftover bits or straddling, and byte addressing lets programs inspect or change any individual character directly.

sections.title: 3. Bytes, Words & Little-Endian Order: Inside the 64 KB Address Space
sections.summary: Unpack the PDP-11's memory layout using the intuitive analogy of a street of numbered post-office boxes. Learn how an 8-bit byte stores a single character or small number ($$0$$ to $$255$$), how two adjacent bytes form an even-aligned 16-bit word, why 16 address wires can name $$2^{16} = 65{,}536$$ individual bytes (a 64 KB address space), and why DEC chose 'little-endian' byte ordering—storing a 16-bit number's least-significant ('little-end') byte at the lower even address and its most-significant ('big-end') byte at the following odd address.

chunks.title: A Long Street of Post-Office Boxes: Bytes and Words
chunks.content_markdown:
Picture a computer's main memory as a long wall of numbered post-office boxes starting at box $$0$$, then box $$1$$, box $$2$$, box $$3$$, and so on. On the earlier PDP-8, each numbered box held a full 12-bit word; if you wanted only half a box (one character), there was no box number for the right-hand half.

The PDP-11 changed the rules by making memory **byte-addressable**. Every single 8-bit **byte**—capable of holding $$2^8 = 256$$ patterns (unsigned numbers $$0$$ to $$255$$, or one ASCII text character like `'A'` or `'7'`)—gets its own unique post-office box number, called its **byte address**.

What happens when the PDP-11 wants to do arithmetic on a full **16-bit word** (which can hold $$2^{16} = 65{,}536$$ patterns)? It simply treats **two adjacent byte boxes** as a single double-wide package! By strict hardware rule, every 16-bit word on the PDP-11 starts at an **even byte address** (such as box $$0$$, $$2$$, $$4$$, or $$100$$) and spans that even byte plus the immediately following odd byte ($$0$$ and $$1$$, $$2$$ and $$3$$, or $$100$$ and $$101$$).

questions.prompt: What does it mean that the PDP-11's memory uses a 'byte-addressable 16-bit word' design?
choices: Every 8-bit byte has its own unique address, and two adjacent bytes combine into a 16-bit word
Only 16-bit words have memory addresses, so individual 8-bit characters cannot be located directly
Each memory address holds sixteen separate 8-bit characters stacked inside a single hardware slot
Memory addresses are written as eight-letter English words rather than binary numbers
questions.explanation: In the PDP-11, every individual 8-bit byte has its own sequential address, while any even-addressed byte and the next odd-addressed byte together form one 16-bit word.

questions.prompt: If a PDP-11 program fetches a full 16-bit word starting at byte address 200, which two byte boxes are accessed together?
choices: Byte address 199 and byte address 200
Byte address 200 and byte address 201
Byte address 200 and byte address 202
Byte address 200 and byte address 216
questions.explanation: A 16-bit word on the PDP-11 always begins at an even byte address (here, 200) and includes the immediately following odd byte address (201).

chunks.title: Why 16 Bits Means a 64-Kilobyte Address Space
chunks.content_markdown:
How many post-office boxes can the PDP-11 processor name if it uses a 16-bit number as a memory address? Let's count the possibilities from first principles.

One binary bit can name $$2^1 = 2$$ boxes (box $$0$$ or box $$1$$). Two bits can name $$2^2 = 4$$ boxes. Every additional bit doubles the number of distinct addresses. With 16 address bits, the processor can generate exactly:
$$2^{16} = 65{,}536 \text{ distinct byte addresses}$$
numbered from byte $$0$$ up to byte $$65{,}535$$.

In computing, because powers of two govern memory wiring, engineers use the unit **kilobyte (KB)** to mean $$2^{10} = 1{,}024$$ bytes (slightly more than a metric thousand). Dividing $$65{,}536$$ by $$1{,}024$$ gives exactly $$64\text{ KB}$$. We call this total range of addressable locations the PDP-11's **64 KB address space**. Since each 16-bit word occupies two bytes, a 64 KB address space equals $$32{,}768$$ (32K) 16-bit words.

questions.prompt: Why does a 16-bit memory address allow a processor to directly name 65,536 bytes (64 KB) of memory?
choices: Because multiplying 16 bits by 4,096 transistor modules equals 65,536 total circuit connections
Because each of the 16 binary bits doubles the number of possible patterns, yielding $$2^{16} = 65{,}536$$
Because the PDP-11 reserves 64 separate memory cabinets that each contain exactly 1,000 decimal bytes
Because every 16-bit word holds 65,536 individual ASCII text characters at the same time
questions.explanation: With 16 binary bits in an address, each bit can independently be 0 or 1, producing $$2^{16} = 65{,}536$$ unique addresses—or $$64 \times 1{,}024 = 64\text{ KB}$$.

questions.prompt: How many full 16-bit words can fit inside the PDP-11's 64 KB (65,536-byte) address space?
choices: Exactly 8,192 words, because each 16-bit word occupies eight consecutive byte addresses
Exactly 16,384 words, because half of every byte must be left empty for parity checking
Exactly 32,768 words, because each 16-bit word occupies two consecutive 8-bit bytes
Exactly 65,536 words, because bytes and 16-bit words share the exact same physical size
questions.explanation: Since each 16-bit word consists of two 8-bit bytes, dividing 65,536 bytes by 2 bytes per word yields 32,768 (32K) 16-bit words.

chunks.title: Which End Goes First? Little-Endian Byte Ordering
chunks.content_markdown:
Once you split a 16-bit word across two consecutive 8-bit byte boxes—say, box $$100$$ and box $$101$$—you face a fascinating design choice. Suppose we have a two-part number like a two-byte integer, which has a **most-significant ('big-end') byte** (worth $$256$$s, like the thousands and hundreds digits in decimal) and a **least-significant ('little-end') byte** (worth $$1$$s, like the tens and ones digits). Which half goes into the lower-numbered box $$100$$?

IBM mainframes placed the 'big end' first at the lower address. DEC's PDP-11 team chose the exact opposite convention: **little-endian byte ordering** (a term later coined by computer scientist Danny Cohen in 1980 after the 'Little-Endians' who cracked eggs at the small end in Jonathan Swift's *Gulliver's Travels*).

Under **little-endian** order on the PDP-11:
- The **even address** (box $$100$$) holds the **low-order (least-significant) byte** (bits $$0$$–$$7$$).
- The **odd address** (box $$101$$) holds the **high-order (most-significant) byte** (bits $$8$$–$$15$$).

questions.prompt: In the PDP-11's 'little-endian' byte ordering, how is a 16-bit word stored across byte addresses 100 and 101?
choices: The high-order (most-significant) byte sits at 100, and the low-order byte sits at 101
The low-order (least-significant) byte sits at 100, and the high-order byte sits at 101
The even bits of the word sit at 100, and the odd bits of the word sit at 101
Both bytes are summed together at 100, while address 101 stores only the positive or negative sign
questions.explanation: Little-endian ordering places the 'little end' (the least-significant byte, bits 0–7) at the lower, even byte address (100) and the 'big end' (the most-significant byte, bits 8–15) at the higher, odd byte address (101).

questions.prompt: Suppose a 16-bit word on a PDP-11 holds the number 515, made of a high-order byte equal to 2 (worth $$2 \times 256 = 512$$) and a low-order byte equal to 3. What is stored at even address 50 and odd address 51?
choices: Address 50 holds 5, and address 51 holds 15
Address 50 holds 2, and address 51 holds 3
Address 50 holds 3, and address 51 holds 2
Address 50 holds 512, and address 51 holds 3
questions.explanation: Because $$515 = (2 \times 256) + 3$$, the least-significant ('little-end') byte is 3 and the most-significant ('big-end') byte is 2. Little-endian order stores 3 at the lower even address (50) and 2 at the next odd address (51).

chunks.title: Why Little-Endian Feels Natural—and Its Odd-Address Trap
chunks.content_markdown:
Why did Gordon Bell and the PDP-11 engineers prefer **little-endian byte ordering**? Imagine the number $$7$$ stored at address $$100$$. As an 8-bit byte at address $$100$$, it holds $$7$$. As a 16-bit word across addresses $$100$$ and $$101$$, its low byte at $$100$$ holds $$7$$ and its high byte at $$101$$ holds $$0$$.

Notice the neat consequence: **whether you read address $$100$$ as an 8-bit byte or as a 16-bit word, the starting address is still $$100$$!** Better yet, when adding multi-word numbers from least-significant byte upward, the processor steps upward through memory addresses ($$100, 101, 102, \dots$$) in the same direction that arithmetic carries propagate.

There is, however, one strict hardware boundary to watch out for on the PDP-11. While you can read or write a single **8-bit byte** at *any* address (even or odd), a full **16-bit word instruction** *must* use an **even address**. If a buggy program asks the PDP-11/20 to fetch a 16-bit word from an odd address like $$101$$, the hardware immediately halts the instruction and triggers a **bus error (odd-address trap)**!

questions.prompt: What practical advantage does little-endian byte ordering offer when a small number (such as 7) is stored in a 16-bit word starting at address 100?
choices: The exact same starting address (100) points to the value 7 whether read as a single byte or a 16-bit word
The processor can skip reading the low-order byte entirely whenever a number is smaller than 100
The high-order byte at address 101 automatically duplicates the value 7 as a backup copy
English words stored in memory are automatically sorted into alphabetical order without software
questions.explanation: Because the least-significant byte sits at the base address (100), reading one byte at address 100 or reading a 16-bit word at address 100 both start at the exact same address and find the value 7.

questions.prompt: What happens on a PDP-11 if a program attempts to execute a 16-bit word operation at an odd byte address such as 101?
choices: The processor silently rounds the address down to 100 and completes the operation normally
The hardware refuses the unaligned word access and triggers an immediate odd-address error trap
The memory controller switches permanently from little-endian mode to big-endian mode
The processor splits the word across three consecutive odd addresses (101, 103, and 105)
questions.explanation: On the PDP-11, 8-bit byte accesses may use even or odd addresses, but 16-bit word accesses must be aligned on even addresses; attempting a word access at an odd address triggers a hardware trap.

chunks.title: A Legacy That Still Runs Inside Your Phone and Laptop
chunks.content_markdown:
Let's step back and admire how cleanly the PDP-11's memory architecture fits together:
- **Byte-addressable 16-bit words:** Every 8-bit byte has its own address, and every even-odd pair of bytes forms a 16-bit word.
- **A 64 KB address space:** Sixteen address bits name $$2^{16} = 65{,}536$$ bytes ($$32{,}768$$ words), eliminating the PDP-8's tiny 128-word memory pages.
- **Little-endian byte ordering:** Within each 16-bit word, the least-significant ('little-end') byte lives at the even address and the most-significant ('big-end') byte lives at the odd address.

If little-endian byte ordering sounds familiar, it should: DEC's later 32-bit VAX, Intel's x86 microprocessors (inside almost every modern PC), and modern ARM chips (inside smartphones and Apple Silicon Macs) all inherited the PDP-11's **little-endian** convention!

Now that we know how bytes and words are arranged in memory, how do those bytes actually travel between the processor, the memory banks, and the outside world? Next, we step onto the PDP-11's shared highway: the **UNIBUS**.

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately connects the PDP-11's memory architecture to modern personal computers and smartphones?
choices: Modern x86 and ARM processors still use the little-endian byte-ordering convention popularized by the PDP-11
Modern laptops are still limited to the exact 65,536-byte total memory capacity of the 1970 PDP-11/20
Modern smartphones have abandoned 8-bit bytes and returned to the 12-bit word size of the PDP-8
Modern processors forbid reading individual bytes and only allow access to 64-byte punch-card blocks
questions.explanation: The little-endian byte-ordering convention established by the PDP-11 was carried forward into DEC's VAX and adopted by Intel x86 and ARM architectures that power modern PCs and smartphones.

questions.prompt: Suppose two ASCII characters, `'H'` (at byte address 400) and `'I'` (at byte address 401), are stored in PDP-11 memory and fetched together as a single 16-bit word at address 400. Where does `'H'` end up inside that 16-bit word?
choices: In the low-order (least-significant) byte, because `'H'` sits at the lower even address 400
In the high-order (most-significant) byte, because `'H'` comes before `'I'` in the alphabet
Split evenly with 4 bits in the low-order byte and 4 bits in the high-order byte
Erased completely, because 16-bit word fetches can only read numeric digits and not letters
questions.explanation: Under little-endian ordering, the byte at the even address (400, containing `'H'`) occupies bits 0–7 (the low-order byte of the 16-bit word), while the byte at the odd address (401, containing `'I'`) occupies bits 8–15.

sections.title: 4. The UNIBUS Highway: Asynchronous Peer-to-Peer Communication
sections.summary: Contrast older computers—which wired memory and peripheral devices onto separate, specialized processor hubs—with the PDP-11's 56-line UNIBUS ribbon highway, where the CPU, core memory, and peripheral controllers plug in as democratic peers. Explore how master-slave bus arbitration lets disk controllers transfer blocks of data directly into memory (Direct Memory Access) without tying up the processor, and how asynchronous handshaking ('master-sync' and 'slave-sync' polite acknowledgments) lets brand-new high-speed memory and slow mechanical teletypes share the exact same highway.

chunks.title: From Tangled Spokes to One Shared Highway
chunks.content_markdown:
Before 1970, the inside of most computers looked like a railroad hub with two incompatible sets of tracks. One thick bundle of wires—the *memory bus*—connected the **Central Processing Unit (CPU)** (the computer's arithmetic and control brain) exclusively to its main memory. A completely separate bundle—the *Input/Output (I/O) bus*—connected the CPU to keyboards, printers, and tape drives.

Because the CPU sat in the middle like a harried telephone switchboard operator, moving data from a tape drive into memory often meant routing every word through the CPU first. Worse, designing a new peripheral meant dealing with special I/O timing and custom cables.

Gordon Bell and Harold McFarland asked a radical question: *What if there is only one road inside the entire computer?* Their answer was the **UNIBUS** (short for *Unified Bus*): a single 56-wire communication highway—carrying 18 address lines, 16 data lines, and 22 control and power-status lines—into which the CPU, memory banks, and every peripheral device plugged side by side as equals.

questions.prompt: How did the PDP-11's UNIBUS depart from the wiring layout of most earlier computers?
choices: It replaced separate memory and I/O buses with a single shared highway connecting the CPU, memory, and devices
It gave every individual peripheral device its own private, dedicated cable directly to every memory chip
It eliminated copper wires altogether and transmitted data across the cabinet using infrared light beams
It combined electrical power and cooling water inside a single hollow brass tube running through the rack
questions.explanation: Whereas traditional designs used one bus for memory and a separate bus for Input/Output peripherals, the UNIBUS connected the processor, memory modules, and all peripheral controllers onto one shared 56-line system bus.

questions.prompt: In the telephone switchboard analogy, what bottleneck plagued older computers that kept memory and I/O on separate buses attached to the CPU?
choices: Memory modules could only store data when all keyboards and printers were physically unplugged
The CPU often had to act as a middleman to shuttle data back and forth between devices and memory
Peripheral devices could talk to each other freely but were unable to send signals to the processor
The processor could only read from memory during the day and write to peripherals at night
questions.explanation: When memory and I/O lived on separate radial buses centered on the CPU, the processor typically had to mediate transfers between peripherals and main memory, consuming valuable CPU time.

chunks.title: Peers on the Highway: Master-Slave Arbitration and DMA
chunks.content_markdown:
If the CPU, the memory modules, a disk drive, and a Teletype all share the single **UNIBUS**, how do they avoid talking over one another at the same time? The UNIBUS solves this with **master-slave bus arbitration**.

At any given microsecond, exactly one device on the UNIBUS wins permission to control the highway; that active initiator is called the **bus master**. The component it chooses to read from or write to—usually a memory board or a device controller—acts as the **bus slave** for that single transaction.

Most of the time, the CPU is the bus master, fetching instructions from memory (its slave). But suppose a spinning magnetic disk needs to load a 1,000-word file into memory. Instead of interrupting the CPU 1,000 times, the disk controller requests the UNIBUS between CPU cycles, temporarily becomes **bus master**, and writes words straight into memory—treating memory as its slave! This peer-to-peer transfer is called **Direct Memory Access (DMA)**, or in DEC manuals, a **Non-Processor Request (NPR)**.

questions.prompt: During a single data transfer on the UNIBUS, what is the difference between the 'bus master' and the 'bus slave'?
choices: The bus master is always the magnetic memory bank, while the bus slave is always the central processor
The bus master supplies electrical power to the rack, while the bus slave cools the cabinet fans
The bus master initiates and controls the transfer, while the bus slave responds to that request
The bus master handles only 8-bit bytes, while the bus slave handles only 16-bit words
questions.explanation: In UNIBUS master-slave arbitration, one component at a time wins control of the bus as the 'master' to initiate a read or write, and the addressed target responds as the 'slave.'

questions.prompt: How does a high-speed disk controller use Direct Memory Access (DMA) on the UNIBUS to load a file into memory?
choices: It halts the computer completely for several minutes while a human operator copies data via paper tape
It forces the CPU to copy every single bit into Register 0 before forwarding it along a private memory wire
It converts binary data into audible clicks that are recorded onto a cassette tape inside the keyboard
It temporarily becomes bus master and writes data words directly to memory without routing each word through the CPU
questions.explanation: Using DMA (which DEC called a Non-Processor Request or NPR), a peripheral controller arbitrates to become bus master for brief bus cycles and transfers data directly to or from memory (the slave) as a peer of the CPU.

chunks.title: No Metronome Required: Asynchronous Handshaking
chunks.content_markdown:
Here is the second stroke of genius inside the UNIBUS: there is **no central clock metronome** forcing every component to march at the same speed. Instead, the UNIBUS uses **asynchronous handshaking**.

Imagine two polite people passing crates across a loading dock. In a *synchronous* (clocked) system, the sender tosses a crate every two seconds on the tick of a metronome—and if the receiver trips and isn't ready, the crate crashes to the floor. In an *asynchronous* handshake, the conversation goes like this:
1. **Master:** Places the address on the bus and raises a signal called **MSYN** (*Master Sync*): 'Hello Slave at address $$200$$, I want to read your word!'
2. **Slave:** Recognizes its address, fetches the data at its own natural speed, places the 16 bits on the data lines, and raises **SSYN** (*Slave Sync*): 'Here is your data!'
3. **Master:** Grabs the data and drops **MSYN** ('Got it, thanks!'), after which the Slave drops **SSYN**.

Because the master simply waits for **SSYN**, a slow $$1{,}000$$-nanosecond memory board and a fast $$300$$-nanosecond semiconductor card can sit side by side on the exact same UNIBUS!

questions.prompt: How does 'asynchronous handshaking' on the UNIBUS coordinate a data transfer between a master and a slave?
choices: The master asserts a request signal (MSYN) and waits until the slave replies with a ready signal (SSYN)
A crystal metronome forces every device on the bus to finish its work in exactly one millisecond
The master sends data three times in a row and hopes the slave catches at least one copy
The slave continuously broadcasts its contents onto the bus whether or not any device asked for them
questions.explanation: Asynchronous handshaking uses interlocking Master Sync (MSYN) and Slave Sync (SSYN) signals: the master initiates the request and waits however long the slave takes to assert SSYN confirming the transfer.

questions.prompt: What major engineering benefit did DEC gain by making the UNIBUS asynchronous rather than locked to a fixed clock speed?
choices: The computer could operate without any electrical power whenever all peripheral devices were idle
Faster new memory boards and slower older peripherals could plug into the same bus without redesigning the system
Programs written for 36-bit IBM mainframes could run on the PDP-11 without being recompiled
The UNIBUS required only a single copper wire instead of a multi-wire ribbon cable
questions.explanation: Because every transfer adapts its duration to the responding slave's SSYN signal, DEC and its customers could mix slow peripherals, standard magnetic core memory, and newer high-speed memory on the same UNIBUS across years of upgrades.

chunks.title: What Happens When Nobody Answers? The Bus Timeout Trap
chunks.content_markdown:
Wait a moment—if an **asynchronous handshake** means the bus master waits patiently for the slave to raise **SSYN** (*Slave Sync*), what happens if a buggy program asks to read from memory address $$120{,}000$$ on a small machine that only has $$16\text{ KB}$$ of memory installed? Since no memory card owns that address, *nobody* will ever raise **SSYN**!

Without a safeguard, the CPU would sit frozen forever waiting for a polite reply from an empty slot. To prevent an eternal lockup, the PDP-11 includes a simple hardware stopwatch on the UNIBUS.

If the CPU asserts **MSYN** and no slave answers with **SSYN** within roughly $$10$$ to $$20$$ microseconds (an eternity in transistor time, where normal answers take less than a microsecond), the hardware stopwatch expires. It aborts the hanging bus cycle and triggers a **bus timeout trap** (vector $$4$$), alerting the operating system or halting the program cleanly so the programmer can see the exact nonexistent address that caused the error.

questions.prompt: On an asynchronous bus where the master waits for a slave's SSYN reply, what happens if the CPU addresses a memory location that is not installed?
choices: The CPU waits indefinitely in a frozen state until a technician physically unplugs the power cord
The nearest installed memory card automatically answers with all ones so the program can keep running
After roughly 10 to 20 microseconds without an SSYN reply, a hardware timer triggers a bus timeout error trap
The Teletype printer immediately punches a replacement memory card out of paper tape
questions.explanation: Because no device responds with SSYN for an unpopulated address, a hardware watchdog timer on the UNIBUS times out after 10–20 microseconds and triggers a bus error trap instead of letting the CPU hang forever.

questions.prompt: Why is a hardware timeout timer essential on an asynchronous bus like the UNIBUS but less critical on a strictly clocked synchronous bus?
choices: Because asynchronous buses run on alternating current that reverses polarity every twenty microseconds
Because synchronous buses cannot connect to more than one memory module at a time
Because asynchronous signals travel at the speed of sound rather than the speed of electricity
Because an asynchronous master explicitly waits for an acknowledgment signal that a missing slave will never send
questions.explanation: On a synchronous bus, a transfer finishes on a fixed clock tick regardless; on an asynchronous bus, the cycle cannot complete until SSYN arrives, so a timeout timer is needed to recover when no slave exists at the requested address.

chunks.title: An Open Invitation to Invent—and a Profound Consequence
chunks.content_markdown:
The **UNIBUS** did more than simplify the wiring inside DEC's Maynard factory—it sparked an entire ecosystem of laboratory innovation. DEC published the UNIBUS electrical and timing rules openly and even sold blank, general-purpose UNIBUS interface cards.

Because of **master-slave bus arbitration** and **asynchronous handshaking**, a graduate student in astronomy, a hospital biomedical engineer, or an industrial robotics startup could build a custom telescope controller or heart-monitor interface and plug it straight into the PDP-11's UNIBUS. As long as their board watched for its address and answered **MSYN** with **SSYN**, the PDP-11 talked to it seamlessly.

And notice the deeper architectural breakthrough hiding in plain sight: on the UNIBUS, a request to read or write a **memory board** and a request to read or write a **peripheral device** use the *exact same address lines, data lines, and MSYN/SSYN handshake*. That means the processor does not even need to know whether an address belongs to memory or to a Teletype! In Section 5, we will see how this insight produced **memory-mapped I/O**.

questions.prompt: How did the UNIBUS help turn the PDP-11 into a favorite platform for university laboratories and third-party equipment makers?
choices: Its published asynchronous handshake let custom lab instruments plug in and communicate using standard bus signals
DEC paid a cash royalty to any university that wired an IBM punch-card reader onto a PDP-11
The UNIBUS required no electronics at all and connected directly to mechanical gears and pulleys
Every PDP-11 shipped with fifty pre-built telescope and medical scanners already installed inside the lid
questions.explanation: Because DEC documented the UNIBUS specification and its forgiving MSYN/SSYN asynchronous handshake, researchers and third-party vendors could easily wire custom instruments straight onto the bus.

questions.prompt: Because memory modules and peripheral controllers share the exact same address, data, and handshake lines on the UNIBUS, what radical simplification becomes possible for the CPU?
choices: The CPU can eliminate all internal registers and store its Program Counter inside the power supply
The CPU can communicate with peripheral devices using ordinary memory addresses instead of special I/O instructions
Memory boards can print text directly onto paper rolls without needing a Teletype or printer
Peripheral devices no longer need distinct addresses because every device responds to address zero
questions.explanation: Since every transaction on the UNIBUS is simply an addressed read or write handshake, the CPU can control Input/Output peripherals simply by reading and writing reserved memory addresses—a technique called memory-mapped I/O.

sections.title: 5. Memory-Mapped I/O: Controlling Hardware Through Reserved Addresses
sections.summary: See how the UNIBUS unlocked one of the PDP-11's signature simplifications: memory-mapped Input/Output (I/O). Instead of needing a separate set of hardware I/O instructions, the PDP-11 sets aside the top 8 KB of its 64 KB address space (the 'I/O page') for device registers. Using concrete examples like reading a Teletype keyboard or spinning up a drive, discover how ordinary memory-read and memory-write instructions inspect a device's Control/Status Register (CSR), move characters through its Data Buffer Register (DBR), and respond to hardware interrupts.

chunks.title: Throw Away the Special I/O Instructions!
chunks.content_markdown:
On the PDP-8 and almost every other computer of the 1960s, talking to the outside world required a completely separate vocabulary of processor instructions. If you wanted to add two numbers in memory, you used normal memory instructions; if you wanted to check whether a human had pressed a key on the Teletype, you had to execute a specialized **Input/Output Transfer (`IOT`)** instruction wired only to the I/O bus.

When Gordon Bell and the PDP-11 team put the CPU, main memory, and peripheral controllers onto the single shared **UNIBUS**, they realized they could throw away special I/O instructions altogether! Their technique is called **memory-mapped I/O**.

In **memory-mapped I/O**, every peripheral device controller—whether a Teletype keyboard, a paper-tape punch, or a magnetic disk drive—is assigned a handful of specific **memory addresses** on the UNIBUS. To send a character to the printer, the CPU simply writes that character's byte to the printer's assigned memory address using an ordinary `MOV` (Move) instruction, just as if it were storing a number in memory!

questions.prompt: What is the core idea behind 'memory-mapped I/O' on the PDP-11?
choices: Peripheral devices are assigned reserved memory addresses and controlled with ordinary memory instructions
Every peripheral device must copy its entire hardware manual into main memory before the processor can boot
The processor uses a separate set of `IOT` instructions that bypass the UNIBUS to reach keyboards and printers
Main memory is physically mounted inside the Teletype cabinet so paper tape can press directly against the wires
questions.explanation: With memory-mapped I/O, device registers sit at reserved addresses on the UNIBUS, allowing the CPU to read and write peripherals using the exact same instructions (`MOV`, `ADD`, `BIT`, `CLR`) used for ordinary memory.

questions.prompt: How did memory-mapped I/O simplify the PDP-11's instruction set compared to earlier machines like the PDP-8?
choices: It reduced the total number of binary digits in a byte from eight bits down to four bits
It allowed the processor to operate without any arithmetic addition or subtraction circuits
It eliminated the need for a separate class of special-purpose Input/Output instructions
It removed the need for memory addresses by broadcasting every character to all devices at once
questions.explanation: Because device registers appear as memory addresses on the UNIBUS, the PDP-11 needed zero special I/O instructions; every existing memory and arithmetic instruction could operate directly on device registers.

chunks.title: Carving Out the Upper 8 KB: The I/O Page
chunks.content_markdown:
If peripheral devices respond to ordinary memory addresses, how does the PDP-11 keep a Teletype from colliding with a program stored in main memory? It divides the **64 KB address space** into two clean neighborhoods.

Out of the $$65{,}536$$ total byte addresses ($$64\text{ KB}$$), the lower $$56\text{ KB}$$—from byte address $$0$$ up to byte address $$57{,}343$$—is reserved for ordinary **main memory**, where your programs and data live. The uppermost **8 KB** of the address space—the top $$8{,}192$$ byte addresses from $$57{,}344$$ to $$65{,}535$$—is permanently set aside as the **I/O page** (also called the *external page*).

Whenever the CPU places an address inside that top $$8\text{ KB}$$ window onto the UNIBUS, main memory stays silent and the peripheral controllers listen up! So on an early PDP-11 without expansion hardware, even if you plugged in $$64\text{ KB}$$ worth of physical memory boards, only $$56\text{ KB}$$ of memory could actually be seen—because the top $$8\text{ KB}$$ of addresses belonged to the **I/O page**.

questions.prompt: How does a basic PDP-11 divide its 64 KB address space between main memory and peripheral devices?
choices: All even addresses belong to main memory, while all odd addresses belong to peripheral devices
The lower 56 KB addresses main memory, while the upper 8 KB forms the reserved I/O page for devices
The lower 32 KB holds peripheral device registers, while the upper 32 KB holds user programs
Every peripheral device shares byte address 0, while bytes 1 through 65,535 belong to main memory
questions.explanation: In the PDP-11's 64 KB address space, the bottom 56 KB (57,344 bytes) maps to physical memory, while the top 8 KB (8,192 bytes) is reserved as the I/O page for device registers and processor control words.

questions.prompt: Why could an unexpanded PDP-11/20 access at most 56 KB of usable main memory even though 16 bits can name 64 KB?
choices: Because 8 KB of every memory board had to be left unpowered to prevent the cabinet from overheating
Because the UNIBUS only had 14 address wires instead of a full set of 16 address wires
Because little-endian byte ordering consumes an extra 8 KB of overhead for every 56 KB of data
Because the top 8 KB of the 64 KB address window was reserved for the I/O page rather than memory
questions.explanation: Since addresses in the upper 8 KB of the 64 KB address space are decoded as the I/O page for peripheral device registers, at most 56 KB of physical memory can be addressed directly in a flat 16-bit space.

chunks.title: Inside a Device Window: CSR and DBR
chunks.content_markdown:
What actually sits at a peripheral's assigned addresses inside the **I/O page**? Typically, a simple device like the console **Teletype Model 33** exposes pairs of 16-bit hardware registers on the UNIBUS: a **Control and Status Register (CSR)** and a **Data Buffer Register (DBR)**.

Think of a pneumatic mail tube at a bank drive-through:
- The **Control and Status Register (CSR)** is the panel of indicator lights and request buttons next to the tube. On the Teletype printer, bit $$7$$ of its CSR is the **Ready (`DONE`) bit**: when bit $$7$$ is $$1$$, the printer is idle and ready to accept a new character; when bit $$7$$ is $$0$$, its mechanical typewheel is still busy clattering across the paper.
- The **Data Buffer Register (DBR)** is the canister slot itself. As soon as the CPU sees that the printer's CSR Ready bit is $$1$$, it executes a simple `MOVB` (*Move Byte*) instruction to drop an 8-bit ASCII code (like $$65$$ for `'A'`) into the printer's **DBR**.

Dropping that byte into the DBR automatically clears the Ready bit to $$0$$ and triggers the Teletype to strike `'A'` onto the paper roll!

questions.prompt: In a typical PDP-11 peripheral interface such as the console Teletype, what are the respective roles of the Control/Status Register (CSR) and the Data Buffer Register (DBR)?
choices: The CSR reports device readiness and control settings, while the DBR holds the actual byte or word transferred
The CSR stores the user's complete text document, while the DBR supplies high-voltage power to the drive motor
The CSR translates English into binary code, while the DBR rewinds the punched paper tape after each printed line
The CSR counts the total number of hours the machine has run, while the DBR cools the internal transistor cards
questions.explanation: A peripheral's CSR contains status flags (such as the Ready/Done bit and Error indicators) and control switches (such as Interrupt Enable), while its DBR holds the actual data character or word being read or written.

questions.prompt: What happens if the CPU writes a sequence of characters into the Teletype printer's Data Buffer Register (DBR) without first checking the Ready bit in its CSR?
choices: The Teletype automatically speeds up its mechanical printhead to match the microsecond speed of the CPU
The fast CPU overwrites characters in the buffer before the slow mechanical printer finishes the first one
The UNIBUS caches all extra characters inside the copper ribbon cable until the printer catches up
The processor converts the extra characters into audible musical tones on the front-panel speaker
questions.explanation: A mechanical Teletype prints only 10 characters per second, whereas the CPU executes hundreds of thousands of instructions per second; checking the CSR Ready bit ensures the previous character has finished printing before loading the next byte into the DBR.

chunks.title: Polling vs. Vectored Interrupts: 'Don't Call Us, We'll Call You'
chunks.content_markdown:
Checking a device's **Control/Status Register (CSR)** over and over in a tight loop—'Are you ready yet? Are you ready yet?'—is called **polling**. Polling is simple to write, but when a Teletype takes a full tenth of a second ($$100{,}000$$ microseconds) to print one letter, a CPU that polls wastes tens of thousands of instruction cycles just staring at bit $$7$$.

To free the processor for useful work, the PDP-11 pairs memory-mapped I/O with **vectored interrupts**. Inside every device's CSR, bit $$6$$ is the **Interrupt Enable (`IE`)** switch. If a program sets bit $$6$$ to $$1$$, the CPU can go off and calculate physics equations while the Teletype prints.

The instant the Teletype finishes printing and its Ready bit flips to $$1$$, the controller tugs an interrupt request line on the UNIBUS and hands the CPU a unique memory address called an **interrupt vector** (for example, address $$60$$ for the keyboard). Unlike the PDP-8, which had to ask every device in turn 'Who just rang the doorbell?', the PDP-11's **vectored interrupt** jumps straight to that specific device's service routine in microseconds!

questions.prompt: Why is enabling interrupts (via bit 6 of a device's CSR) usually much more efficient than polling bit 7 in a loop?
choices: Interrupts make the mechanical printhead of a Teletype move ten times faster across the paper roll
Polling requires a human operator to press a front-panel button after every single printed letter
Interrupts let the CPU execute other work and respond only when the slow device signals it is ready
Polling erases the contents of main memory whenever the Teletype runs out of paper tape
questions.explanation: Instead of wasting hundreds of thousands of CPU cycles repeatedly testing the CSR Ready bit while a slow peripheral works, enabling interrupts allows the CPU to run other code until the device signals completion.

questions.prompt: What advantage did the PDP-11's 'vectored interrupts' have over the simpler interrupt system of the PDP-8?
choices: Vectored interrupts allow the computer to run without any software interrupt handler routines in memory
Every peripheral device shares a single interrupt wire that halts the processor until rebooted
The CPU ignores all interrupts during daytime hours and processes them in a single batch at midnight
The interrupting device supplies its own unique vector address, jumping the CPU straight to its handler
questions.explanation: On the PDP-8, an interrupt forced the CPU to poll devices in software to discover which one requested service; on the PDP-11, the interrupting device transmits a dedicated vector address on the UNIBUS so the CPU jumps straight to the right handler.

chunks.title: One Unified World of Addresses
chunks.content_markdown:
Take a moment to appreciate how **memory-mapped I/O** and the **UNIBUS** lock the first half of the PDP-11's architecture into a single, harmonious picture:
- **One address space:** Out of $$64\text{ KB}$$ of addresses, the bottom $$56\text{ KB}$$ is main memory and the top $$8\text{ KB}$$ is the **I/O page**.
- **Zero special I/O instructions:** Every peripheral exposes a **Control/Status Register (CSR)** and **Data Buffer Register (DBR)** at fixed addresses in the I/O page. Want to clear a device buffer? Use `CLR` (*Clear*). Want to test its Ready bit? Use `TSTB` (*Test Byte*) or `BIT` (*Bit Test*).
- **Polite interrupts when needed:** Flip the Interrupt Enable bit in the CSR, and the device notifies the CPU via a dedicated UNIBUS interrupt vector.

Now that we see how data sits in memory and flows to peripherals across the UNIBUS, where does the CPU actually hold and manipulate those bytes and words while a program runs? In Section 6, we step inside the processor itself to meet its eight 16-bit workbenches: **registers `R0` through `R7`**.

questions.prompt: Because of memory-mapped I/O, which instruction can a PDP-11 programmer use to reset a peripheral device's Data Buffer Register to zero?
choices: The standard `CLR` (Clear) memory instruction aimed at the device register's address in the I/O page
A special `IOTZ` (Input/Output Zero) instruction that only works on external teleprinter cables
A hardware-only punch-card command that cannot be executed from stored memory programs
No instruction at all, because device registers inside the I/O page are strictly read-only
questions.explanation: Because device registers are mapped into the address space just like memory locations, any standard instruction—such as `CLR` to zero a word or `MOV` to load a value—works directly on a peripheral register.

questions.prompt: How do the UNIBUS, the 64 KB address space, and memory-mapped I/O work together when a PDP-11 prints a character?
choices: The CPU switches from the memory bus to a separate I/O cable and sends a 12-bit `IOT` pulse to address 0
The CPU writes the character to the printer's DBR address in the upper 8 KB I/O page over the UNIBUS
The printer becomes bus master, erases the lower 56 KB of memory, and reads the character from a punch card
The CPU halts its clock until an operator flips the front-panel toggle switches to match the ASCII code
questions.explanation: To print a character, the CPU simply executes a memory write to the printer's DBR address in the upper 8 KB I/O page, and that write travels across the UNIBUS using the standard MSYN/SSYN handshake.

sections.title: 6. Eight Workbenches: General-Purpose Registers R0–R7, the PC & the Stack
sections.summary: Step inside the PDP-11 processor to examine its eight 16-bit general-purpose registers (R0 through R7)—high-speed internal workbenches that eliminated the constant memory shuffling of single-accumulator machines. Learn how R0–R5 hold numbers or memory pointers interchangeably, while R6 and R7 perform architectural magic by doubling as the hardware Stack Pointer (SP, managing a last-in, first-out stack of return addresses and local data in memory) and the Program Counter (PC, pointing to the next instruction to fetch).
introduced_terms: Program Counter as a general register (PC / R7)

chunks.title: From One Cramped Workbench to Eight: Registers R0–R7
chunks.content_markdown:
Remember the carpenter's workshop analogy from Section 2? On the 12-bit PDP-8, the processor had only **one** internal workbench—its single accumulator—forcing programs to constantly shuffle intermediate numbers back and forth to slower main memory across the bus.

When Gordon Bell and his team redesigned the PDP-11, they equipped the processor with **eight 16-bit general-purpose registers**, named **`R0`, `R1`, `R2`, `R3`, `R4`, `R5`, `R6`, and `R7`**. Built out of fast transistor memory latches (called *flip-flops*) right inside the CPU, a register can be read or updated in a fraction of the time it takes to talk to main memory over the UNIBUS.

Why are they called **general-purpose registers**? Because on many earlier computers, one register could only do arithmetic (an *accumulator*), while another register could only hold memory addresses (an *index register*). On the PDP-11, **any register from `R0` to `R7`** can hold a 16-bit number, an 8-bit byte, an array counter, or a 16-bit memory pointer (address) with complete symmetry!

questions.prompt: Why are the PDP-11's eight internal 16-bit registers (`R0` through `R7`) described as 'general-purpose registers'?
choices: Because any of the registers can be used interchangeably to hold data values, counters, or addresses
Because they are mounted on the outside of the cabinet where any visitor in the room can flip them
Because each register automatically converts between binary, decimal, and Roman numerals in hardware
Because they are shared simultaneously by eight separate computers connected across a telephone line
questions.explanation: Unlike older architectures that split internal storage into dedicated accumulators and restricted index registers, any PDP-11 register (`R0`–`R7`) can perform arithmetic or serve as a memory address pointer.

questions.prompt: What performance advantage does a processor gain by keeping frequently used variables and pointers inside `R0`–`R5` instead of main memory?
choices: Values stored in `R0`–`R5` expand automatically from 16 bits to 64 bits of mathematical precision
Internal CPU registers operate much faster than fetching and storing words across the UNIBUS to memory
Internal CPU registers never require electricity and retain their contents when the building loses power
Using internal registers allows the UNIBUS to disconnect from the power supply during calculations
questions.explanation: Registers `R0`–`R7` are built from fast high-speed logic directly inside the CPU, so register-to-register operations avoid the time cost of UNIBUS handshakes with external memory.

chunks.title: The Cafeteria Tray Dispenser: R6 as the Hardware Stack Pointer (SP)
chunks.content_markdown:
While registers `R0` through `R5` are free for whatever scratch values or pointers your program needs, the last two registers—**`R6`** and **`R7`**—pull brilliant double duty. They are full members of the eight general-purpose registers, yet the CPU hardware also wires them to two essential housekeeping jobs.

First, **`R6`** serves as the **hardware Stack Pointer (`SP`)**. Imagine a spring-loaded stack of cafeteria trays: when you **push** a clean tray onto the top, the stack sinks down by one notch; when you **pop** a tray off the top, you always get the *most recently added* tray first (a **Last-In, First-Out** or **LIFO** structure).

On the PDP-11, `R6` (`SP`) holds the memory address of the current top of a stack in main memory that grows **downward** from high memory addresses toward low memory addresses. Whenever your program calls a helper subroutine—or whenever a Teletype interrupt suddenly arrives—the PDP-11 hardware automatically uses `R6` to **push** the return address onto the stack so the CPU remembers exactly where to resume afterward!

questions.prompt: What special hardware role is assigned to general-purpose register `R6` on the PDP-11?
choices: It serves as the permanent Teletype buffer, holding the last two ASCII characters typed by the user
It stores the fixed serial number of the processor and cannot be modified by any instruction
It serves as the hardware Stack Pointer (SP), tracking the top of a last-in, first-out memory stack
It counts the electrical frequency of the wall outlet to keep the room's wall clock accurate
questions.explanation: Register `R6` is the hardware Stack Pointer (`SP`), which points to the active top of a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) stack in memory used for subroutine return addresses, interrupts, and temporary data.

questions.prompt: Why is a hardware-managed Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) stack so helpful when Subroutine A calls Subroutine B, which then calls Subroutine C?
choices: The stack automatically runs all three subroutines at the exact same microsecond on separate buses
The stack deletes Subroutine A from memory so Subroutine C can use its post-office boxes forever
A LIFO stack guarantees that subroutines can only be called in alphabetical order from A to Z
Each nested call pushes its return address on top, and finishing in reverse order pops each caller back
questions.explanation: Because nested subroutine calls finish in the exact reverse order they were started (C finishes back to B, then B finishes back to A), pushing return addresses onto a LIFO stack and popping them on return handles arbitrary nesting and recursion naturally.

chunks.title: The Bookmark in the Recipe: R7 as the Program Counter (PC)
chunks.content_markdown:
