If `R6` being the Stack Pointer is clever, DEC's choice for **`R7`** is pure architectural poetry: **`R7` is the processor's Program Counter (`PC`)**!

What is a **Program Counter**? Think of following a printed recipe step by step: your finger points to the line you are about to read next. Inside any computer, the **Program Counter (`PC`)** is the register holding the memory address of the **next instruction word** the CPU is about to fetch and execute. Since every PDP-11 instruction is made of one to three 16-bit words (2 bytes per word), each time the CPU fetches a 16-bit word of an instruction, it automatically adds $$2$$ to `R7` (`PC`) so it points to the next word.

On almost every earlier computer, the Program Counter was a hidden, private register that ordinary arithmetic instructions could not touch. On the PDP-11, **the Program Counter is simply Register 7**! Any instruction that can modify `R0` can also modify `R7`. Want to jump to a new program address stored in `R0`? Just move `R0` into `R7`: `MOV R0, R7`!

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental job of the Program Counter (`PC` / `R7`) while a PDP-11 program is running?
choices: It holds the memory address of the next instruction word that the processor is about to fetch
It counts the total number of programs that have been run since the computer was manufactured
It measures the temperature of the magnetic core memory in degrees Celsius
It stores the password of the currently logged-in operator inside the upper I/O page
questions.explanation: Like a bookmark or finger tracking the next step in a recipe, the Program Counter (`PC`, which is Register `R7` on the PDP-11) always holds the memory byte address of the next instruction word to be fetched.

questions.prompt: Because the Program Counter is simply general-purpose register `R7` on the PDP-11, what happens if a program executes `ADD #6, R7` (adding 6 to `R7`)?
choices: The processor halts with an illegal-register error because `R7` is hidden from arithmetic instructions
The processor skips forward by 6 bytes (three 16-bit words) in the instruction stream, performing a jump
The processor runs the exact same instruction six times in a row before moving to the next line
The UNIBUS increases its voltage by 6 volts to speed up the attached Teletype printer
questions.explanation: Since `R7` *is* the Program Counter, adding 6 to `R7` directly advances the address of the next instruction by 6 bytes, causing the CPU to branch forward over three 16-bit words.

chunks.title: Why Every Stack Word Must Stay Even-Aligned
chunks.content_markdown:
Here is a subtle detail about **`R6` (`SP`)** and **`R7` (`PC`)** that connects directly back to Section 3's rule about even byte addresses.

Remember that on the PDP-11, every **16-bit word** in memory—including every machine instruction word and every 16-bit return address pushed onto the stack—must start at an **even byte address** ($$0, 2, 4, \dots$$). Attempting to fetch a 16-bit word from an odd byte address triggers an immediate **odd-address trap**.

Think about what that means for `R7` (`PC`) and `R6` (`SP`):
1. Because every instruction is a 16-bit word (or a sequence of 16-bit words), **`R7` (`PC`) must always remain an even number** (`...0` in binary).
2. Because hardware interrupts and subroutine calls can happen at any microsecond and always push full 16-bit words onto the stack using **`R6` (`SP`)**, **`R6` must also always stay aligned on an even byte address**! Even if you push or pop a single 8-bit byte using `R6`, the PDP-11 hardware automatically adjusts `R6` by **$$2$$ bytes** instead of $$1$$ so the stack pointer never becomes odd!

questions.prompt: Why must both the Stack Pointer (`R6`) and the Program Counter (`R7`) always contain even byte addresses on the PDP-11?
choices: Because the PDP-11's arithmetic unit is physically incapable of representing odd numbers in binary
Because odd addresses in every memory module are reserved exclusively for the Teletype keyboard
Because instructions and stacked words are 16-bit words, which hardware requires to start at even addresses
Because the UNIBUS only wires the even-numbered registers (`R0`, `R2`, `R4`, `R6`) to main memory
questions.explanation: Since instructions fetched via `R7` (`PC`) and return addresses/status words pushed via `R6` (`SP`) are 16-bit words, and 16-bit words on the PDP-11 must be aligned on even byte boundaries, both `R6` and `R7` must stay even.

questions.prompt: How does the PDP-11 hardware protect the Stack Pointer (`R6`) if a programmer executes a single-byte instruction that pushes or pops via `R6`?
choices: It ignores the instruction completely and turns on a red warning lamp on the front panel
It copies the byte into all eight registers (`R0`–`R7`) to balance the electrical load
It temporarily switches the entire computer into 8-bit Desk Calculator mode for ten seconds
It automatically steps `R6` by 2 bytes instead of 1 byte so `R6` remains aligned on an even boundary
questions.explanation: Even during a byte operation, the PDP-11 hardware special-cases `R6` (`SP`) so that stepping it automatically changes its address by 2 rather than 1, guaranteeing the stack pointer never lands on an odd address right before an interrupt.

chunks.title: Eight Registers, Unlimited Possibilities
chunks.content_markdown:
Let's review the PDP-11's internal register file—a design so clean that computer science textbooks taught it as a model of clarity for decades:
- **Eight 16-bit general-purpose registers (`R0`–`R7`):** Fast internal CPU workbenches that replace the PDP-8's lone accumulator.
- **`R0` through `R5`:** Completely interchangeable registers for holding arithmetic values, text character pairs, loop counters, or memory pointers.
- **`R6` (`SP` — Stack Pointer):** General-purpose register that doubles as the hardware pointer to the top of a downward-growing Last-In, First-Out stack in memory.
- **`R7` (`PC` — Program Counter):** General-purpose register that doubles as the address of the next instruction word to fetch.

Now comes the best part: why did making `R6` (the Stack Pointer) and `R7` (the Program Counter) ordinary members of `R0`–`R7` pay off so handsomely? Because when you combine those eight registers with the PDP-11's **orthogonal instruction set** and **auto-increment/auto-decrement addressing modes**, magic happens. Let's see how in Section 7!

questions.prompt: How did the PDP-11's register layout (`R0`–`R7`) compare to how earlier minicomputers handled their accumulator, stack, and program counter?
choices: It unified eight general workbenches with the Stack Pointer (`R6`) and Program Counter (`R7`) in one set
It eliminated the Program Counter and Stack Pointer entirely so programmers had to track addresses on paper
It provided a single 12-bit accumulator and required magnetic tape reels to hold subroutine return addresses
It locked each of the eight registers to a single peripheral device inside the upper 8 KB I/O page
questions.explanation: Instead of treating the accumulator, index registers, stack pointer, and program counter as separate, incompatible hardware islands, the PDP-11 unified them into eight symmetrical 16-bit registers (`R0`–`R7`).

questions.prompt: When a PDP-11 program calls a subroutine or handles an interrupt, how do `R6` (`SP`) and `R7` (`PC`) work together?
choices: The contents of `R6` and `R7` are added together and written to the Teletype Data Buffer Register
The return address in `R7` is pushed onto the stack pointed to by `R6`, and `R7` loads the new routine's address
Both `R6` and `R7` are cleared to zero so the subroutine can start from byte address 0
Register `R6` becomes the new Program Counter while `R7` permanently shuts down until the machine reboots
questions.explanation: To enter a subroutine or interrupt handler without losing its place, the CPU pushes the return address from `R7` (`PC`) onto the stack addressed by `R6` (`SP`) and loads the target routine's starting address into `R7` (`PC`).

sections.title: 7. Orthogonal Instructions & Auto-Increment/Decrement Addressing
sections.summary: Discover why programmers celebrated the PDP-11's instruction set as an 'orthogonal' design where virtually any operation (such as moving, adding, or comparing either 16-bit words or 8-bit bytes) works symmetrically with any register and any addressing mode. Walk through how auto-increment `(Rn)+` and auto-decrement `-(Rn)` addressing automatically step a register pointer forward or backward by 1 byte or 2 bytes per access—making stack pushes, stack pops, string loops, immediate constants, and relocatable position-independent code effortless.

chunks.title: What Does 'Orthogonal' Mean in an Instruction Set?
chunks.content_markdown:
Imagine ordering lunch at a restaurant with a frustrating, arbitrary menu: 'You can get soup only if you sit at Table 1, you can get a sandwich only on Tuesdays at Table 2, and toast cannot be ordered with soup.' That was what programming most 1960s computers felt like: the `ADD` instruction worked only with the accumulator, the `LOOP` instruction worked only with Register B, and moving data between two memory locations took three separate steps.

Gordon Bell and his team designed the PDP-11 around the opposite ideal: **instruction orthogonality** (from the geometry word for perpendicular, independent axes—meaning *what operation you perform* and *where the data lives* can be chosen independently!).

On the PDP-11, a two-operand instruction like `MOV src, dst` (*Move source to destination*) or `ADD src, dst` splits cleanly into an **operation code** plus two symmetric 6-bit **operand specifiers**. Each 6-bit specifier picks **any of the 8 registers (`R0`–`R7`)** and **any of 8 addressing modes**. Even better, slapping a `B` onto the instruction name (`MOVB`, `CMPB`, `CLRB`) performs the exact same operation on an **8-bit byte** instead of a 16-bit word!

questions.prompt: In computer architecture, what does 'instruction orthogonality' mean on the PDP-11?
choices: Circuit boards inside the cabinet must be mounted at strict 90-degree angles to prevent magnetic interference
Almost any instruction operation can be combined freely with any register (`R0`–`R7`) and any addressing mode
Each instruction can only operate on one fixed register that is permanently wired to that opcode
Programs must be written in square grids of exactly sixteen columns by sixteen rows on paper tape
questions.explanation: Instruction orthogonality means the choice of operation (such as `MOV`, `ADD`, `SUB`, `CMP`) is independent of the choice of register (`R0`–`R7`) and addressing mode (how the operand is located in registers or memory).

questions.prompt: Because both the source and destination of a PDP-11 `MOV` or `ADD` instruction can use any addressing mode, what can a single PDP-11 instruction do that required three instructions on a single-accumulator machine?
choices: It can sort an entire 2.5-megabyte magnetic disk pack alphabetically without using the UNIBUS
It can multiply sixteen separate numbers together inside the power supply at the same time
It can copy or add directly from one memory location (or device register) to another in a single instruction
It can translate an entire FORTRAN program into printed English documentation in one clock cycle
questions.explanation: On a single-accumulator machine, copying or adding memory A to memory B required loading A into the accumulator, adding B, and storing back; on the orthogonal PDP-11, `MOV A, B` or `ADD A, B` does it in one clean instruction.

chunks.title: Pointers That Step Themselves: Auto-Increment and Auto-Decrement
chunks.content_markdown:
How does a 6-bit operand specifier tell the PDP-11 *where* to find data? Three bits choose one of the eight registers (`R0`–`R7`), and the other three bits choose one of **eight addressing modes**.

Mode `0` (**Register mode**, written `R0`) simply uses the number sitting inside `R0`. Mode `1` (**Register Deferred mode**, written `(R0)`) treats the number inside `R0` as a *memory address pointer*—fetching the post-office box that `R0` points to.

Then come the two modes that made PDP-11 programmers cheer: **auto-increment** and **auto-decrement addressing**:
- **Auto-increment `(Rn)+`:** Use the address inside register `Rn` to fetch or store your data, and **then automatically step `Rn` forward** to the next item! (It adds $$1$$ for a byte instruction like `MOVB`, or adds $$2$$ for a 16-bit word instruction like `MOV`.)
- **Auto-decrement `-(Rn)`:** **First step `Rn` backward** (subtract $$1$$ for a byte, or subtract $$2$$ for a word), and **then** use that new address to fetch or store your data!

questions.prompt: Suppose register `R1` holds byte address 500, and the PDP-11 executes the 8-bit byte instruction `MOVB (R1)+, R0`. What happens?
choices: The byte at address 500 is copied into `R0`, and `R1` automatically increments by 1 to become 501
Register `R1` first increments to 501, and then the byte at address 501 is copied into `R0`
The number 500 itself is copied into `R0`, and memory address 500 is erased to zero
The 16-bit word at 500 is copied into `R0`, and `R1` automatically decrements by 2 to become 498
questions.explanation: In auto-increment mode `(R1)+`, the processor first accesses the memory location currently pointed to by `R1` (500) and then increments `R1` by the operand size (1 byte for `MOVB`, leaving `R1` at 501—ready for the next character in a string!).

questions.prompt: How does the step size of auto-increment `(Rn)+` automatically adapt between `MOVB` (Move Byte) and `MOV` (Move Word) for registers `R0`–`R5`?
choices: It always adds 16 to `Rn` regardless of whether the instruction manipulates bytes or words
It adds 2 for byte instructions and subtracts 2 for word instructions to keep memory balanced
It requires the programmer to type a separate `ADD` instruction after every memory access
It adds 1 to `Rn` after a byte instruction (`MOVB`) and adds 2 to `Rn` after a 16-bit word instruction (`MOV`)
questions.explanation: Because each byte occupies 1 address and each 16-bit word occupies 2 addresses, auto-increment automatically advances `Rn` by 1 on byte instructions and by 2 on word instructions so `Rn` always points to the very next element.

chunks.title: Effortless Stacks and String Loops
chunks.content_markdown:
Watch what happens when we combine **auto-decrement `-(Rn)`** and **auto-increment `(Rn)+`** with Section 6's **Stack Pointer (`SP`, which is `R6`)**!

Remember that the PDP-11 stack in memory grows **downward** toward lower addresses, and `SP` (`R6`) always points to the item currently sitting on top of the stack:
- To **push** the contents of `R0` onto the stack, you just write: `MOV R0, -(SP)`. In one instruction, `SP` steps down by $$2$$ bytes to an empty slot and stores `R0` there!
- To **pop** the top word off the stack back into `R0`, you just write: `MOV (SP)+, R0`. It reads the top word at `SP` and steps `SP` back up by $$2$$ bytes!

Because of **orthogonality**, `R6` isn't the only register that can run a stack—*any* register `R0`–`R5` can manage its own private data stack using `-(Rn)` and `(Rn)+`! And if you want to copy a text string byte-by-byte from a pointer in `R1` to a pointer in `R2`, a single instruction—`MOVB (R1)+, (R2)+`—copies the character *and* advances both pointers at once!

questions.prompt: On the PDP-11 (where the stack grows downward toward lower addresses), which pair of instructions pushes `R0` onto the hardware stack and later pops it back into `R0`?
choices: Push with `MOV R0, (SP)+` (auto-increment) and pop with `MOV -(SP), R0` (auto-decrement)
Push with `MOV R0, -(SP)` (auto-decrement) and pop with `MOV (SP)+, R0` (auto-increment)
Push with `CLR R6` (clear stack) and pop with `ADD R6, R7` (add stack to program counter)
Push and pop require dedicated `PUSH` and `POP` opcodes that work only on the hidden accumulator
questions.explanation: Since `SP` (`R6`) points to the current top word of a downward-growing stack, `MOV R0, -(SP)` first decrements `SP` by 2 to allocate a new top slot and stores `R0`, while `MOV (SP)+, R0` reads that top word and increments `SP` by 2 to reclaim the slot.

questions.prompt: What does the single PDP-11 instruction `MOVB (R1)+, (R2)+` accomplish when `R1` points to a source text string and `R2` points to a destination buffer?
choices: It swaps the memory addresses inside `R1` and `R2` without touching main memory at all
It erases both text strings to zero and halts the processor at the end of the line
It copies one 8-bit character from `(R1)` to `(R2)` and advances both `R1` and `R2` to the next byte
It adds the two memory addresses together and stores the sum inside the Program Counter
questions.explanation: Thanks to orthogonality and auto-increment addressing on both operands, `MOVB (R1)+, (R2)+` fetches the byte at `R1`, increments `R1` by 1, writes the byte to `R2`, and increments `R2` by 1—all in one instruction.

chunks.title: The Ultimate Trick: Using Modes with R7 (The Program Counter)
chunks.content_markdown:
Now prepare for the most delightful surprise in the entire PDP-11 architecture. What happens if you use **auto-increment mode `(Rn)+`** or **indexed mode `X(Rn)`** when the register `Rn` is **`R7`—the Program Counter (`PC`)**?

1. **Immediate constants (`#n` is really `(PC)+`):** Suppose you write `MOV #42, R0` to load the constant number $$42$$ into `R0`. The PDP-11 doesn't need a special 'load constant' instruction! Instead, the assembler places the word $$42$$ right after the `MOV` instruction in memory and encodes the source operand as `(R7)+`—auto-incrementing the Program Counter! When the CPU runs the instruction, `R7` (`PC`) is pointing right at the word $$42$$; `(R7)+` fetches $$42$$ into `R0` and steps `R7` forward by $$2$$ bytes so the CPU neatly skips over the constant to the next instruction!
2. **Position-Independent Code (`X(PC)`):** By addressing variables as a signed offset added to `R7` (`PC`), a program refers to data as *'the word 50 bytes ahead of wherever I am right now.'* That means the entire program—called **position-independent code (PIC)**—can be loaded at *any* address in memory and run without changing a single bit!

questions.prompt: How does the PDP-11 implement an 'immediate constant' (such as `MOV #42, R0`) without needing a special hardware addressing mode just for constants?
choices: It places 42 in the word immediately following the instruction and uses auto-increment on `R7` (`(PC)+`) to fetch and skip past it
It stores a permanent table of every possible 16-bit number inside the Teletype keyboard controller
It pauses the program and waits for a human operator to toggle the number 42 on the front panel
It adds the number 1 to Register 0 forty-two separate times in a hidden hardware loop
questions.explanation: Because `R7` is the Program Counter (`PC`), encoding the source operand as `(R7)+` fetches the constant stored in the word right after the instruction opcode and automatically increments `PC` by 2 so execution continues at the next instruction.

questions.prompt: Why does 'PC-relative addressing' (locating data by adding an offset to `R7` / `PC`) make it easy to write 'position-independent code' (PIC)?
choices: Because PC-relative programs run entirely inside the eight CPU registers without ever using main memory
Because the UNIBUS automatically rewires the physical memory cards whenever a program moves
Because position-independent code is allowed to use odd byte addresses for 16-bit words without trapping
Because distances between instructions and nearby data stay the same no matter where the block of code is loaded in memory
questions.explanation: When a program references targets as offsets relative to the current Program Counter (`R7`), moving the entire program block to a different starting address in memory preserves every relative distance—so the code runs anywhere without modification.

chunks.title: Why C Programmers Fell in Love with the PDP-11
chunks.content_markdown:
Step back and look at what **instruction orthogonality**, **auto-increment `(Rn)+`**, **auto-decrement `-(Rn)`**, and **`R6`/`R7` symmetry** created:
- A processor where almost every instruction (`MOV`, `ADD`, `SUB`, `CMP`, `BIT`, `BIC`, `BIS`, `CLR`, `INC`, `DEC`, `TST`) works uniformly on words or bytes across all registers and memory.
- Built-in pointer stepping (`(Rn)+` and `-(Rn)`) that turns stack pushes, stack pops, and array or string traversal into single instructions.
- Clever reuse of `R7` (`PC`) so immediate constants and **position-independent code** emerge for free from standard addressing modes.

As we will explore in Part II of this series, when Dennis Ritchie and Ken Thompson at Bell Labs developed the **C programming language** and **Unix** on a PDP-11 in the early 1970s, C's famous pointer expressions—like `'p++'` (use pointer `'p'`, then increment it) and `'--p'` (decrement pointer `'p'`, then use it)—mapped effortlessly onto the PDP-11's `(Rn)+` and `-(Rn)` modes!

Next, in Section 8, let's leave abstract instructions behind and touch the physical hardware of a 1970s PDP-11 lab: magnetic core memory and RK05 disk packs.

questions.prompt: Which C programming language idioms correspond directly to the PDP-11's auto-increment `(Rn)+` and auto-decrement `-(Rn)` addressing modes?
choices: Conditional `switch` statements and floating-point `double` division
Pointer post-increment (`*p++`) and pointer pre-decrement (`*--p`)
Preprocessor `#include` directives and multiline comments
Global `struct` declarations and `goto` labels targeting line numbers
questions.explanation: Dereferencing a pointer and stepping it forward (`*p++`) or stepping a pointer backward and dereferencing it (`*--p`) match the exact behavior of the PDP-11's `(Rn)+` and `-(Rn)` addressing modes.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures why the PDP-11's addressing modes and register file are considered a landmark of clean computer architecture?
choices: By creating a separate dedicated instruction for every possible combination of device and memory page, the PDP-11 had over 10,000 unique opcodes
By restricting all arithmetic to a single 12-bit accumulator, the PDP-11 prevented programmers from accidentally modifying pointers in memory
By making `SP` (`R6`) and `PC` (`R7`) general registers and pairing them with orthogonal modes, a few simple rules unlocked stacks, constants, and relocatable code
By forbidding byte operations in registers, the PDP-11 forced all text processing to happen inside external punch-card sorters
questions.explanation: Rather than bolting on dozens of special-case instructions, the PDP-11 achieved extraordinary expressive power—stacks, immediate values, absolute addresses, and PC-relative position-independent code—just by applying 8 orthogonal addressing modes across 8 registers that included `SP` and `PC`.

sections.title: 8. Magnetic Core Memory, Condition Codes & the RK05 Disk Pack
sections.summary: Explore the physical storage technologies and status flags that gave 1970s PDP-11 labs their unmistakable character. Understand how the Processor Status Word (PSW) tracks negative, zero, overflow, and carry condition codes alongside interrupt priorities; how planes of tiny hand-strung ferrite rings ('magnetic core memory') remember bits even when unplugged via destructive read-restore cycles; and how the pizza-box-sized RK05 removable disk cartridge (2.5 MB on a 14-inch aluminum platter) let individual users carry their own operating systems and data onto the machine.
introduced_terms: Processor Status Word (PSW) and condition codes

chunks.title: The CPU's Mood Ring: The Processor Status Word (PSW)
chunks.content_markdown:
Before we look at the physical memory and disks attached to a PDP-11, we need to meet one last internal CPU register that guides every decision a program makes: the 16-bit **Processor Status Word (`PSW`)**.

Whenever the PDP-11 executes an instruction like `SUB` (*Subtract*), `CMP` (*Compare*), or even `MOV` (*Move*), how does a following branch instruction know whether the result was zero, negative, or too large to fit in 16 bits? The CPU automatically updates four single-bit flags at the bottom of the **Processor Status Word**, called **condition codes**:
- **`N` (Negative):** Set to $$1$$ if the result's sign bit (bit $$15$$ for a word, bit $$7$$ for a byte) is $$1$$ (negative).
- **`Z` (Zero):** Set to $$1$$ if the result was all zeros ($$0$$).
- **`V` (Overflow):** Set to $$1$$ if signed arithmetic overflowed past the largest positive or negative number.
- **`C` (Carry):** Set to $$1$$ if addition or subtraction carried or borrowed out of the highest bit.

In keeping with **memory-mapped I/O**, even the CPU's own **PSW** has a reserved address at the very top of the I/O page!

questions.prompt: What is the role of the four condition codes (`N`, `Z`, `V`, `C`) inside the PDP-11's Processor Status Word (PSW)?
choices: They record whether the latest result was negative, zero, overflowed, or carried so branches can decide
They control the speed of the four cooling fans mounted at the top of the 19-inch equipment rack
They indicate which of the four operators in the room currently holds the physical key to the console
They permanently store the first four letters of the user's login name inside the power supply
questions.explanation: The `N` (Negative), `Z` (Zero), `V` (Overflow), and `C` (Carry) condition code bits in the PSW are updated automatically by arithmetic, logical, and data-movement instructions, allowing subsequent branch instructions (`BEQ`, `BMI`, `BCS`, etc.) to test the outcome.

questions.prompt: Alongside the four condition codes, the Processor Status Word (PSW) holds a 3-bit CPU priority level (0 through 7). How does DEC expose the PSW to software?
choices: It requires a technician to remove the backplane cover and move four brass jumpers with pliers
It maps the PSW to a reserved address at the top of the I/O page so normal instructions can access it
It prints the PSW onto punched paper tape after every single arithmetic instruction
It hides the PSW completely so that no software program or operating system can ever inspect it
questions.explanation: True to the PDP-11's memory-mapped design philosophy, the CPU's own Processor Status Word (PSW) is assigned the highest word address in the upper 8 KB I/O page, allowing system software to inspect or change CPU status and interrupt priority using normal instructions.

chunks.title: Tiny Magnetized Donuts: How Magnetic Core Memory Works
chunks.content_markdown:
When you bought a PDP-11/20 in 1970, where did its bytes and words physically live? Not on silicon memory chips—which were still tiny, expensive, and experimental—but inside **magnetic core memory**.

If you looked through a magnifying glass at a PDP-11 core memory board (such as an `MM11` module), you would see a fine wire screen woven with thousands of microscopic dark rings—called **cores**—each pressed from iron-oxide (ferrite) powder and barely the size of a pencil tip. Every single tiny donut stores **one binary bit**!

Passing an electric current along the intersecting horizontal ($$X$$) and vertical ($$Y$$) wires threading a donut magnetizes the ring either **clockwise (say, $$1$$)** or **counterclockwise ($$0$$)**. And here is a property that astonishes modern computer users whose RAM forgets everything the instant power fails: **magnetic core memory is non-volatile**! Because each ferrite ring is a permanent little magnet, you could switch off a PDP-11 on Friday evening, turn it back on Monday morning, and your program was still sitting intact in memory!

questions.prompt: How does magnetic core memory physically store a single binary bit (0 or 1)?
choices: By trapping a microscopic drop of mercury inside a sealed glass tube on the circuit board
By punching or not punching a rectangular hole into a strip of oiled paper tape inside the CPU
By magnetizing a tiny ferrite ring in a clockwise or counterclockwise direction via threaded wires
By spinning a miniature brass flywheel either forward or backward at ten thousand revolutions per minute
questions.explanation: In magnetic core memory, each bit is a tiny donut-shaped ferrite core threaded by thin copper wires; electric currents magnetize the ring clockwise or counterclockwise to represent 1 or 0.

questions.prompt: Why is magnetic core memory described as 'non-volatile' compared to modern computer RAM?
choices: It is submerged in fireproof mineral oil so the memory boards can never overheat during summer months
It automatically backs up every byte to an IBM mainframe over the telephone line every five seconds
Its contents cannot be changed by the CPU once written and behave like a permanent read-only vinyl record
Its ferrite rings retain their magnetic orientation and stored data even when electrical power is turned off
questions.explanation: Because the clockwise or counterclockwise magnetization of ferrite cores persists without electricity, magnetic core memory preserves its contents across power-offs (assisted by power-fail circuits that stop mid-cycle writes cleanly).

chunks.title: The Read-Restore Dance: Why Reading a Core Destroys It!
chunks.content_markdown:
There is a fascinating physical catch to **magnetic core memory**: how do you check whether a silent little ferrite ring is magnetized clockwise ($$1$$) or counterclockwise ($$0$$)? By the laws of electromagnetism, a stationary magnetic field induces *zero* voltage in a wire; you only get an electrical pulse in a **sense wire** when a core's magnetic field **flips**!

So to **read** a bit from core memory, the memory controller deliberately sends a current pulse that forces the core into the **$$0$$ (counterclockwise) state**:
- If the core was already $$0$$, nothing flips, and the sense wire stays quiet (CPU reads a $$0$$).
- If the core was a $$1$$, its magnetism **flips from $$1$$ to $$0$$**, inducing a sharp voltage pulse on the sense wire (CPU reads a $$1$$)—**but in the process, the $$1$$ inside the core was just erased to $$0$$**!

This is called a **destructive read**. To keep memory from losing its data every time it is read, every core-memory read cycle on the PDP-11 automatically finishes with a second half-cycle—a **restore (rewrite) pulse**—that immediately flips any $$1$$ bits right back to $$1$$!

questions.prompt: Why is reading a bit from magnetic core memory inherently a 'destructive read' that requires an immediate restore cycle?
choices: Detecting a 1 requires flipping the core to 0 to induce a sense pulse, which erases the 1 unless rewritten
Reading a core melts the copper wire threading the ring, requiring an automated soldering iron to repair it
The UNIBUS deliberately zeroes out all memory modules after every instruction as a security precaution
Cosmic rays in the laboratory flip every magnetic core to 0 whenever the cabinet door is opened
questions.explanation: Because a sense wire only detects a *changing* magnetic field, the controller reads a core by pulsing it to the 0 state; if it held a 1, the flip generates a read pulse but leaves the core at 0, so the controller immediately performs a restore cycle to write the 1 back.

questions.prompt: Why did PDP-11 power supplies include 'power-fail/auto-restart' sensors that warned the CPU a few milliseconds before wall power died?
choices: So the Teletype could type a ten-page farewell letter to the operator before the lights went out
So the memory controller could finish any active read-restore cycle instead of leaving a word erased
So the magnetic cores could dump all their bits onto punched cards before losing their magnetism
So the operator would have enough time to run across the room and catch the spinning disk platter
questions.explanation: Although magnetic cores hold their state without power, losing electricity *halfway* through a destructive read—after the read pulse flipped 1s to 0s but before the restore pulse put them back—would corrupt that word, so PDP-11 power supplies gave enough warning to finish the cycle cleanly.

chunks.title: From Paper Tape to the Pizza Box: The RK05 Disk Pack
chunks.content_markdown:
Even non-volatile magnetic core memory cost roughly a dollar per word in the early 1970s, meaning a typical PDP-11 had only $$8\text{ KB}$$ to $$32\text{ KB}$$ of core memory. Where did users keep their operating systems, compilers, and data files?

On the cheapest setups, programs lived on rolls of punched **paper tape** or small bidirectional magnetic tape reels called **DECtape**. Loading a large assembler from paper tape on a Teletype at $$10$$ bytes per second could take half an hour of deafening clatter!

Everything changed when a lab added DEC's iconic **RK05 disk drive**. A programmer walked into the computer room carrying a round, white plastic cartridge the size of a large pizza box—an **RK05 removable disk pack**. Inside that protective shell sat a single $$14\text{-inch}$$ spinning aluminum platter coated with magnetic oxide. You slid the cartridge into the front slot of the RK05 drive, flipped the rocker switch to **RUN**, waited for the platter to spin up to $$1{,}500\text{ rpm}$$ and the read/write heads to float on a microscopic cushion of filtered air, and suddenly had **$$2.5\text{ megabytes}$$** of fast random-access storage!

questions.prompt: How did the RK05 removable disk pack change daily life in a 1970s university or research PDP-11 lab?
choices: It allowed a single paper tape roll to hold 500 gigabytes of uncompressed high-definition video
It replaced the UNIBUS with a wireless radio link that beamed files across the university campus
Each user could slide in their own 2.5 MB cartridge holding their personal operating system and files
It eliminated the need for electricity by spinning the aluminum platter with a hand-cranked spring
questions.explanation: Because the RK05 drive accepted removable 2.5 MB 14-inch single-platter cartridges, different students or research teams sharing one PDP-11 could each mount their own bootable disk pack in minutes.

questions.prompt: Why did an RK05 disk drive require strict air filtration and wait until the 14-inch platter spun up to 1,500 rpm before loading the read/write heads?
choices: The spinning platter acted as the primary air-conditioning fan for the entire room's mainframe cabinets
The magnetic oxide coating only became magnetic when heated to 100 degrees Celsius by air friction
Filtered air was used to blow punched paper chads out of the track holes etched into the aluminum disc
The heads floated on a microscopic cushion of air, so a dust particle or slow spin could cause a crash
questions.explanation: Inside an RK05 drive, the aerodynamic read/write heads flew on a tiny boundary layer of air mere millionths of an inch above the 1,500 rpm platter; smoke or dust could wedge under a head and gouge the magnetic coating in a catastrophic 'head crash.'

chunks.title: A Complete Physical System—Wait, How Do We Start It?
chunks.content_markdown:
Picture yourself standing in a 1972 laboratory in front of a six-foot-tall DEC cabinet:
- Inside the CPU, the **Processor Status Word (`PSW`)** tracks condition codes (`N`, `Z`, `V`, `C`) and interrupt priority levels.
- Plugged into the **UNIBUS** are heavy **magnetic core memory** modules whose tiny hand-threaded ferrite rings store bits non-volatilely through a sub-microsecond read-restore dance.
- Mounted in the rack above is an **RK05 disk drive**, humming softly as your personal $$2.5\text{ MB}$$ removable cartridge spins up and its **READY** light glows white.

Now comes a practical puzzle that every new PDP-11 operator faced. Suppose you walk up to a freshly delivered PDP-11—or one whose core memory was wiped by a runaway program—and you want it to load the operating system off your spinning **RK05 disk pack**. Today's computers have a permanent startup chip (ROM/BIOS) that automatically knows how to read the disk. Early PDP-11s often had **no startup ROM at all**! How do you teach an empty computer to read its own disk? In Section 9, you will toggle those instructions in by hand!

questions.prompt: Which three components work together when a running PDP-11 transfers a block of files from an RK05 disk pack into main memory?
choices: The RK05 controller becomes UNIBUS master via DMA and writes 16-bit words into magnetic core memory
The Processor Status Word physically spins the RK05 platter while the Teletype punches each sector onto paper tape
A human operator reads each bit from a magnifying glass over the ferrite cores and types it onto the keyboard
The CPU disconnects the UNIBUS and copies one bit per second through the condition code flags
questions.explanation: Once commanded via its memory-mapped registers in the I/O page, the RK11/RK05 disk controller uses UNIBUS DMA (master-slave arbitration) to stream words directly from the spinning platter into magnetic core memory.

questions.prompt: What puzzle faced an operator trying to start an early PDP-11 whose magnetic core memory was blank and that lacked a permanent startup ROM chip?
choices: Magnetic core rings could not accept any electric current until they were preheated for two hours with a hair dryer
The CPU had no instructions in memory telling it how to command the disk or tape drive to load the system
The RK05 disk drive refused to spin its platter unless the operating system was already running on the Teletype
The UNIBUS address wires remained disconnected until an IBM mainframe sent an unlock signal over the phone line
questions.explanation: Without a permanent ROM bootstrap, a blank core memory contains no instructions telling the CPU which I/O page addresses to write to start an RK05 disk or paper-tape read—so the operator had to enter a short 'bootstrap loader' program manually.

sections.title: 9. Blinking Lights & Toggle Switches: Octal Math and the Front-Panel Console
sections.summary: Sit down at the iconic purple-and-red bezel of a PDP-11 front panel to learn how engineers communicated directly with bare hardware. See why 16-bit binary numbers were grouped into 3-bit octal (base-8) digits (`0` through `7`) matching the color-coded clusters of paddle switches, and walk step-by-step through toggling an octal bootstrap loader into the Switch Register using `LOAD ADRS`, `DEP` (Deposit), `EXAM` (Examine), and `START` so the machine can read its operating system off paper tape or an RK05 disk.
introduced_terms: front-panel console (Switch Register, LOAD ADRS, and DEP)

chunks.title: Why Three Bits at a Time? Octal (Base-8) Notation
chunks.content_markdown:
If you look at the famous purple-and-red plastic bezel of a PDP-11 **front-panel console**, your eyes are immediately drawn to a long horizontal row of plastic paddle switches at the bottom and rows of glowing red indicator lamps above them. Why are those switches painted in alternating three-switch color blocks—purple, red, purple, red, purple?

Because reading a raw 16-bit binary string like `0000010111000110` is a recipe for human eye strain and typos! Instead, DEC engineers used **octal (base-8) switch grouping**. Starting from the rightmost bit (bit $$0$$), you group a 16-bit word into **five 3-bit clusters** plus **one leftover top bit** (bit $$15$$).

Why 3 bits per group? Because three binary bits (worth $$4$$, $$2$$, and $$1$$) can represent $$2^3 = 8$$ values—the single octal digit **`0` through `7`**:
- `000` = `0`, `001` = `1`, `010` = `2`, `011` = `3`
- `100` = `4`, `101` = `5`, `110` = `6`, `111` = `7`

Even better, remember that inside a PDP-11 instruction, a register (`R0`–`R7`) is chosen by **3 bits** and an addressing mode (`0`–`7`) is chosen by **3 bits**! So in **octal**, every register number and every addressing mode shows up as its own readable single digit!

questions.prompt: Why were the toggle switches on a PDP-11 front panel painted in alternating three-switch color groups representing octal (base-8) digits?
choices: Because each 3-bit cluster maps to one digit `0`–`7`, matching the 3-bit register and mode fields
Because three switches were required to control the red, green, and blue beams of a color television
Because the UNIBUS could only transmit three binary bits per second across the laboratory floor
Because federal electrical codes required high-voltage switches to be separated into groups of three
questions.explanation: Three binary bits have $$2^3 = 8$$ combinations (`0`–`7`), making octal notation both effortless to flip by hand on 3-switch color blocks and a direct match for the 3-bit addressing mode and 3-bit register specifiers inside PDP-11 instructions.

questions.prompt: When a 16-bit PDP-11 word is written as a six-digit octal number (from `000000` to `177777`), why can the leftmost digit only be `0` or `1`?
choices: Because the leftmost switch on every PDP-11 front panel was glued down at the Maynard factory
Because octal numbers are forbidden by mathematics from starting with any digit larger than 1
Because values starting with `2` through `7` are reserved exclusively for 36-bit IBM mainframes
Because five 3-bit octal digits cover 15 bits, leaving only a single top bit (bit 15) for the leftmost digit
questions.explanation: Grouping 16 bits from the right into 3-bit octal digits produces five full 3-bit groups ($$5 \times 3 = 15$$ bits) plus one remaining most-significant bit (bit 15), which can only be `0` or `1`.

chunks.title: Hands on the Paddles: Switch Register, LOAD ADRS, EXAM, and DEP
chunks.content_markdown:
Let's sit down at the **front-panel console** and learn what its switches and lights actually do. Across the bottom sit 16 (or on larger models, 18) numbered data switches called the **Switch Register** (up = $$1$$, down = $$0$$). To their right sit six action paddles:

1. **`HALT` / `ENABLE`:** Flipping this switch down halts the CPU between instructions so you can inspect or edit memory safely.
2. **`LOAD ADRS` (Load Address):** Flip a 16-bit octal address onto the **Switch Register** paddles and press `LOAD ADRS`. The top row of red **ADDRESS** lights immediately glows with your chosen post-office box number!
3. **`EXAM` (Examine):** Press `EXAM`, and the console reads the 16-bit word stored at that address in magnetic core memory, lighting up the bottom row of red **DATA** lamps.
4. **`DEP` (Deposit):** Flip a new 16-bit octal number onto the Switch Register and lift the spring-loaded `DEP` paddle upward. That 16-bit word is written straight into core memory at the displayed address!

Conveniently, pressing `EXAM` or lifting `DEP` repeatedly **auto-increments the console address by $$2$$ bytes**, letting you walk through consecutive 16-bit words without touching `LOAD ADRS` again!

questions.prompt: Which sequence of front-panel actions allows an operator to store the octal word `012700` into magnetic core memory at octal address `001000`?
choices: Set `012700` on the switches, press `START`, and then turn the console key to the `LOCK` position
Set `001000` on the switches and press `LOAD ADRS`, then set `012700` on the switches and lift `DEP`
Press `EXAM` sixteen times in a row while holding down both the `HALT` and `CONT` paddles
Flip all switches down to zero and wait for the Teletype paper-tape punch to load the address
questions.explanation: To store a word from the front panel, you first enter the target address (`001000`) on the Switch Register and press `LOAD ADRS`, then enter the data word (`012700`) on the Switch Register and lift `DEP` (Deposit).

questions.prompt: Why does lifting the `DEP` (Deposit) or pressing the `EXAM` (Examine) switch repeatedly advance the console's target address by 2 after each step?
choices: Because odd-numbered addresses inside magnetic core memory cannot store binary zeros
Because the console is wired to skip over every other instruction in a program to save electricity
Because each deposited or examined item is a 2-byte word, so stepping by 2 moves to the next word
Because two operators are expected to take turns flipping switches at opposite ends of the panel
questions.explanation: Since each 16-bit word occupies 2 byte addresses on the PDP-11, automatically stepping the console address by 2 on consecutive `DEP` or `EXAM` actions lets an operator load or inspect a whole sequence of program words rapidly.

chunks.title: Pulling Yourself Up by Your Bootstraps: The Bootstrap Loader
chunks.content_markdown:
Now we can solve the puzzle from the end of Section 8: how do you start an empty PDP-11 when its core memory has no instructions telling it how to read the paper-tape reader or the **RK05 disk pack**? You toggle in a **front-panel bootstrap loader**!

The phrase comes from the tall tale of Baron Munchausen pulling himself out of a swamp by his own bootstraps. A **bootstrap loader** (from which we get the modern everyday word **'booting' a computer**) is a tiny, self-contained program—often just **$$6$$ to $$14$$ words long**—kept on a laminated wallet card in every PDP-11 programmer's shirt pocket.

To boot from an RK05 disk, you flipped `HALT`, set starting address `001000`, pressed `LOAD ADRS`, and rhythmically toggled in a handful of octal words with `DEP`—instructions that pointed a register at the RK05 controller's **Control/Status Register** in the **I/O page**, commanded the drive to read Sector $$0$$ (the *boot block*) into memory address $$0$$ via **UNIBUS DMA**, and looped until the transfer finished. Then you loaded `001000`, flipped `ENABLE` and `START`, and watched the disk boot the full operating system!

questions.prompt: What is the job of a 'front-panel bootstrap loader' toggled into a PDP-11 by hand?
choices: It is a tiny 6-to-14-word program that tells a disk or tape drive to read the operating system into memory
It is a full 56-kilobyte FORTRAN compiler that must be entered on the switches before every user job
It is a hardware routine that demagnetizes all ferrite cores so the cabinet power supply can cool down
It is an encryption password that unlocks the glass door of the computer room for the night shift
questions.explanation: A front-panel bootstrap loader is a minimal sequence of machine instructions (typically 6 to 14 words) toggled into core memory to trigger the peripheral controller (such as an RK05 disk or paper-tape reader) to load the rest of the operating system.

questions.prompt: Why could an RK05 disk bootstrap loader on the PDP-11 be written in as few as six to eight 16-bit octal words?
choices: Because the RK05 drive automatically understood spoken English commands through a console microphone
Because memory-mapped I/O and DMA let a few `MOV` instructions point the controller at memory and start a read
Because octal digits compress a thousand lines of assembly code into a single 3-bit switch setting
Because the operating system was already permanently wired inside Register 0 through Register 5
questions.explanation: Because the RK05's registers sit in the memory-mapped I/O page and the controller can DMA an entire disk sector straight into memory at address 0 once triggered, just a few `MOV` instructions suffice to kick off the boot read.

chunks.title: Reading the Blinking Lights—and the Console Switch Register Address
chunks.content_markdown:
Once you flipped `START` and the PDP-11 began executing millions of cycles, the front panel turned into a living dashboard. Experienced operators did not view those **blinking lights** as mere decoration—they could **read the machine's state at a glance**!

Because the **ADDRESS** and **DATA** lamps glowed brighter for addresses where the CPU spent most of its time, a seasoned programmer could tell immediately whether the operating system was sitting in its normal idle loop, waiting on an I/O device inside the upper **I/O page** (when the top three address lights `177...` burned steady red), or stuck in a tight crash loop at a low memory address.

And here is one last front-panel delight: the physical **Switch Register** paddles on the front panel were *themselves* wired into **memory-mapped I/O** at octal address `177570`! A running program could read `177570` at any time to check which switches the human had flipped up or down, and anything the program wrote to `177570` lit up the **DATA** lamps—turning the front panel into a live interactive game controller or status display!

questions.prompt: How could an experienced PDP-11 operator tell from the front-panel lights whether the processor was accessing peripheral devices in the I/O page?
choices: The bottom Switch Register paddles physically flipped themselves up and down using electric motors
The cabinet emitted a loud bell chime every time an even memory address was read
The upper address lights glowed steadily (`177...`), showing accesses in the top 8 KB I/O window
All red indicator lamps on the front panel turned bright green whenever a disk transfer started
questions.explanation: Since the upper 8 KB I/O page occupies the highest addresses (`160000`–`177777` in octal), frequent accesses to device registers made the high-order address lamps on the front panel glow noticeably.

questions.prompt: How did DEC integrate the physical front-panel Switch Register and DATA display lamps into the PDP-11's programming model?
choices: They could only be read when the CPU was completely halted and unplugged from the UNIBUS
They required a dedicated 80-column punch-card reader to copy switch settings into Register 7
They were wired exclusively to the power supply to adjust the room's fluorescent lighting
They were mapped to address `177570` in the I/O page so programs could read switches and light lamps
questions.explanation: The console Switch/Display Register was memory-mapped at octal address `177570` in the I/O page: reading `177570` returned the current position of the 16 toggle switches, and writing to `177570` displayed a 16-bit pattern on the DATA lights.

chunks.title: Hardware ROMs Arrive—and a Bigger Ceiling Looms
chunks.content_markdown:
Toggling an octal **bootstrap loader** into the **Switch Register** with `LOAD ADRS` and `DEP` was a rite of passage for an entire generation of computer scientists—so ingrained that many could still recite the octal numbers for the RK05 boot loader decades later! Eventually, DEC offered plug-in UNIBUS cards (such as the `BM792` diode ROM and later the `M9301` and `M9312` bootstrap/terminator modules) containing permanent **Read-Only Memory (ROM)** so an operator could boot simply by pressing a button or typing a two-letter device code like `DK`.

By 1972, the PDP-11 had conquered laboratories, factories, and universities around the world. Yet its very triumph brought DEC face to face with a new architectural ceiling.

Instead of one scientist running one small experiment, universities wanted **dozens of students** logged into a single PDP-11 at the same time from interactive terminals, running big compilers, databases, and operating systems. How can twenty users share a machine whose 16-bit addresses can only name **$$64\text{ KB}$$** ($$56\text{ KB}$$ of memory plus the $$8\text{ KB}$$ I/O page)? In our final section, Section 10, we will see how the **PDP-11/45** and **PDP-11/70** shattered the $$64\text{ KB}$$ barrier!

questions.prompt: What convenience did plug-in UNIBUS ROM cards (such as the `BM792` or `M9301`) add to later PDP-11 installations?
choices: They held permanent bootstrap loader code in read-only memory so operators did not have to toggle it in
They converted the 16-bit PDP-11 processor into a 64-bit supercomputer without changing the CPU
They replaced the spinning RK05 disk platter with a roll of self-inking typewriter ribbon
They eliminated the need for the UNIBUS by wiring the Teletype directly to the power cord
questions.explanation: Plug-in bootstrap ROM cards held the short disk and tape loader routines permanently in read-only memory mapped into the I/O page, allowing one-step booting without manually toggling octal words on the Switch Register.

questions.prompt: What growing demand in the early-to-mid 1970s pushed the PDP-11 architecture up against the limit of its 16-bit (64 KB) address space?
choices: New ASCII characters grew from 8 bits to 128 bits per letter, filling all memory with a single word
Multi-user time-sharing systems and larger programs needed far more than 56 KB of physical memory at once
Magnetic core rings shrank so much that each board could hold only 100 bytes instead of 8 KB
The UNIBUS timeout timer shortened to zero microseconds whenever more than one user typed
questions.explanation: As PDP-11s were pressed into service for multi-user time-sharing labs and sophisticated operating systems, keeping multiple users and large programs in memory simultaneously required expanding physical memory well beyond 56 KB.

sections.title: 10. Breaking the 64 KB Barrier: The PDP-11/45, PDP-11/70 & Split I/D Spaces
sections.summary: Conclude Part I by examining how the PDP-11's runaway popularity collided with the ceiling of its 16-bit (64 KB) address space as multi-user time-sharing systems grew. Trace how the fast PDP-11/45 (1972) and the flagship PDP-11/70 (1975) introduced a hardware Memory Management Unit (MMU) to translate 16-bit virtual addresses into 18-bit (256 KB) or 22-bit (4 MB) physical memory, paired with Separate Instruction and Data (I/D) spaces and Kernel/Supervisor/User protection rings—laying the hardware foundation for RSX-11, RSTS/E, Bell Labs Unix, the C language, and the global computing legacy explored in Part II.
introduced_terms: Memory Management Unit (MMU) and virtual-to-physical translation
Kernel, Supervisor, and User protection modes (PDP-11/45 & 11/70)

chunks.title: The 16-Bit Dilemma: How Do You Grow Without Breaking Existing Programs?
chunks.content_markdown:
Imagine you are Gordon Bell's engineering team in 1971. Customers love the PDP-11/20, and thousands of programs are already written for its 16-bit registers (`R0`–`R7`). Now universities and corporate labs are begging for a faster PDP-11 that can hold **$$256\text{ KB}$$** or even **$$4\text{ megabytes}$$** of memory so twenty users can run programs at the same time.

Here is the architectural dilemma: every register (`R0`–`R7`), every pointer, and every address calculation inside a PDP-11 program is **16 bits wide**! And as we learned in Section 3, a 16-bit number can only count up to $$2^{16} = 65{,}536$$ bytes ($$64\text{ KB}$$).

If you widen all the registers to 24 or 32 bits, every existing PDP-11 program breaks. So how do you let each running program keep using familiar **16-bit addresses** while allowing the physical machine to plug in **hundreds of kilobytes or megabytes** of memory? You place an electronic translator—called a **Memory Management Unit (`MMU`)**—between the CPU and the main memory bus!

questions.prompt: Why couldn't DEC simply widen registers `R0`–`R7` from 16 bits to 32 bits on the 1972 PDP-11/45 to address more memory?
choices: Because changing the register and word size would break compatibility with existing 16-bit PDP-11 software
Because 32-bit binary numbers had not yet been discovered by academic mathematicians in 1972
Because magnetic core memory rings could only be magnetized in fixed 16-bit physical groups
Because the Teletype Model 33 keyboard would overheat if connected to a 32-bit internal register
questions.explanation: The entire PDP-11 instruction set, word layout, and software ecosystem were built around 16-bit words and 16-bit registers (`R0`–`R7`); preserving binary compatibility required keeping program addresses 16 bits wide while translating them in hardware.

questions.prompt: Where does a hardware Memory Management Unit (MMU) sit, and what is its high-level purpose?
choices: It sits inside the Teletype printer and converts lowercase ASCII letters into uppercase letters
It sits between the CPU and memory, translating a program's 16-bit addresses into wider physical addresses
It sits inside the RK05 disk cartridge and scrubs dust particles off the spinning aluminum platter
It replaces registers `R0` through `R7` with a single 12-bit accumulator when memory is full
questions.explanation: Positioned between the CPU core and the physical memory bus, the MMU intercepts the 16-bit 'virtual' addresses generated by a running program and translates them on the fly into wider physical memory addresses.

chunks.title: Hotel Room Numbers vs. Building Floors: Virtual-to-Physical Translation
chunks.content_markdown:
How does a **Memory Management Unit (`MMU`)**—introduced on the high-speed **PDP-11/45** in 1972—turn a 16-bit address into an **18-bit physical UNIBUS address** (naming $$2^{18} = 262{,}144$$ bytes, or **$$256\text{ KB}$$**)?

Think of an office building where three small startup companies each rent a suite of eight rooms. Inside its own suite, *every* company numbers its doors `Room 0` through `Room 7`. When Alice at Company A walks toward `Room 2`, the building receptionist checks a directory table: *'Company A's Room 2 is actually on Floor 14, Suite 1402.'* When Bob at Company B asks for `Room 2`, the receptionist sends him to *'Floor 29, Suite 2902.'*

On the PDP-11:
- The 16-bit address inside your program (`0` to `64 KB`) is called a **virtual address**, divided into **eight 8 KB 'pages'** (chosen by the top 3 bits of the 16-bit address).
- For each of those 8 pages, the **MMU** holds a **Page Address Register (`PAR`)** and a **Page Descriptor Register (`PDR`)** that translate that 8 KB virtual page into *any* slice of the larger **physical address space**!

questions.prompt: In the PDP-11 Memory Management Unit (MMU), what is the difference between a 'virtual address' and a 'physical address'?
choices: Virtual addresses are used only by the Teletype, while physical addresses are used only by the disk drive
Virtual addresses are always odd numbers, while physical addresses are always even numbers
A virtual address is the 16-bit address seen by a program, while a physical address is the actual hardware location
A virtual address is stored on punched paper tape, while a physical address is toggled on the front panel
questions.explanation: A running program continues to use 16-bit virtual addresses (0–64 KB) in `R0`–`R7`, and the MMU's Page Address Registers translate those virtual page numbers into 18-bit (256 KB) or 22-bit (4 MB) physical memory addresses.

questions.prompt: How does the MMU allow five different user programs in a time-sharing lab to all be compiled to start at virtual address `000000` without overwriting each other?
choices: It erases the other four programs to paper tape every microsecond the CPU adds two numbers
It forces four of the five users to wait outside the building until the first user logs off
It compresses all five programs into a single 8-bit byte at physical address zero
It maps each user's virtual page 0 to a different, non-overlapping region of physical memory
questions.explanation: Just as two companies can each have a 'Room 0' on different floors of a skyscraper, the operating system loads different Page Address Register tables into the MMU for each user, mapping each user's virtual address `000000` to its own private block of physical memory.

chunks.title: Doubling Each Program's Room: Split Instruction and Data (I/D) Spaces
chunks.content_markdown:
Giving the machine $$256\text{ KB}$$ of physical memory via an **MMU** was great for keeping several different programs in memory at once. But what if **one single program**—like a big compiler or scientific simulation—needed more than $$64\text{ KB}$$ for itself?

To double the working room of a single program on the **PDP-11/45** and **PDP-11/70**, DEC's engineers invented a clever trick called **split Instruction and Data (`I/D`) spaces**.

Notice that every time the CPU touches memory, it knows *why* it is asking:
- Is it fetching an **instruction word** via `R7` (the **Program Counter**)?
- Or is it reading/writing a **data variable or stack word** via an operand address?

With **split I/D spaces** turned on, the MMU maintains **two separate sets of eight page registers**: one mapping table for **Instruction (`I`) space** and a completely separate mapping table for **Data (`D`) space**! When `PC` (`R7`) fetches code at address `002000`, the MMU looks up `002000` in **I-space**; when that instruction reads a variable at address `002000`, the MMU looks up `002000` in **D-space**—giving one program **$$64\text{ KB}$$ of code PLUS $$64\text{ KB}$$ of data ($$128\text{ KB}$$ total)**!

questions.prompt: How does 'split Instruction and Data (I/D) space' on the PDP-11/45 and PDP-11/70 allow a single program to use up to 128 KB of memory using only 16-bit addresses?
choices: The MMU routes instruction fetches through one 64 KB map (I-space) and data accesses through a second 64 KB map (D-space)
The CPU glues two 16-bit registers (`R0` and `R1`) together to form a single 32-bit Program Counter
The UNIBUS runs twice as fast during daytime hours so each memory board holds twice as many bits
Programmers write half of their program in binary and the other half in octal on the front panel
questions.explanation: Because the CPU distinguishes instruction fetches via `PC` (`R7`) from data operand accesses, the MMU can direct instruction addresses through an 8-page I-space map (64 KB) and data addresses through a separate 8-page D-space map (64 KB), totaling 128 KB per process.

questions.prompt: When split I/D space is active on a PDP-11/45 or PDP-11/70, what happens if an instruction sitting at virtual address `004000` executes `MOV 004000, R0`?
choices: The processor halts immediately because instructions and data may never use the same virtual number
The instruction is fetched from I-space `004000`, while `MOV` reads its data word from a separate D-space `004000`
The instruction overwrites itself with zeros and erases the contents of Register 0
The MMU turns off virtual memory and resets the entire computer back to PDP-11/20 mode
questions.explanation: Under split I/D spaces, virtual address `004000` in I-space (used when `PC` fetches the instruction) and virtual address `004000` in D-space (used when `MOV` reads its data operand) map through different MMU registers to two distinct physical memory locations.

chunks.title: Protection Modes and the Legendary 1975 PDP-11/70
chunks.content_markdown:
If twenty students are sharing one PDP-11, what stops a student's buggy program from changing the **MMU** page registers, writing straight into the **I/O page** to wipe the **RK05** disk, or executing a `HALT` instruction that freezes everyone else's terminal?

To enforce strict safety boundaries, the **PDP-11/45** added three hardware privilege rings tracked inside the **Processor Status Word (`PSW`)**: **Kernel mode**, **Supervisor mode**, and **User mode** (each with its own separate hardware **Stack Pointer `R6`** and its own MMU page tables!).
- Only the trusted operating system running in **Kernel mode** is mapped to the upper 8 KB **I/O page**, allowed to adjust MMU tables, or permitted to execute `HALT`.
- Ordinary student programs run in restricted **User mode**: if a User program tries to touch another user's memory or write to a read-only page, the MMU blocks the access and traps cleanly to the Kernel!

In 1975, DEC crowned the family with the legendary **PDP-11/70**: expanding physical addressing to **22 bits ($$4\text{ megabytes}$$)**, adding a fast **2 KB cache memory** (an ultra-fast transistor buffer holding recently accessed words right next to the CPU), and introducing a high-speed **MASSBUS** for large disks alongside the classic UNIBUS!

questions.prompt: Why did the PDP-11/45 and PDP-11/70 provide separate Kernel, Supervisor, and User modes in the Processor Status Word (PSW)?
choices: So three different operators could flip the front-panel toggle switches at the exact same time
So the machine could run IBM, Honeywell, and Data General programs without recompiling
So the Kernel operating system could protect the I/O page, MMU tables, and other users from User programs
So the power supply could step down smoothly from 220 volts to 110 volts to 12 volts
questions.explanation: By running ordinary programs in unprivileged User mode—where their MMU tables exclude the I/O page and other users' physical memory, and privileged instructions trap—the Kernel operating system stays safe from buggy or malicious user code.

questions.prompt: How much physical memory could the flagship 1975 PDP-11/70 address using its 22-bit physical address space?
choices: Up to 64 kilobytes ($$2^{16}$$ bytes) of magnetic core memory
Up to 256 kilobytes ($$2^{18}$$ bytes) of paper-tape storage
Up to 1 megabyte ($$2^{20}$$ bytes) of Teletype buffer memory
Up to 4 megabytes ($$2^{22}$$ bytes) of physical memory
questions.explanation: With 22 physical address bits ($$2^{22} = 4{,}194{,}304$$ bytes), the PDP-11/70 expanded physical memory capacity to 4 megabytes and added a fast 2 KB cache and high-speed MASSBUS storage controllers.

chunks.title: From Maynard's Woolen Mill to the Dawn of Modern Software
chunks.content_markdown:
Look how far we have traveled in Part I of our PDP-11 journey! Starting in 1957 inside a Civil War woolen mill in Maynard, Massachusetts, Ken Olsen, Harlan Anderson, Gordon Bell, and DEC's engineers challenged the closed-door priesthood of **batch-processing mainframes** with the hands-on **interactive minicomputer**.

When the 12-bit, single-accumulator PDP-8 hit a ceiling in the age of 8-bit ASCII text, the 1970 **PDP-11/20**—and its big siblings, the **PDP-11/45** and **PDP-11/70**—introduced an architecture of enduring elegance:
- **Byte-addressable 16-bit words** in **little-endian** order across a **64 KB virtual address space** (expanded to **256 KB** and **4 MB** via the **MMU** and **split I/D spaces**).
- The peer-to-peer asynchronous **UNIBUS** and **memory-mapped I/O** inside the upper 8 KB **I/O page**.
- **Eight general-purpose registers (`R0`–`R7`)**—with `R6` as the **Stack Pointer** and `R7` as the **Program Counter**—paired with **orthogonal instructions** and **auto-increment/decrement** modes.

In **Part II**, we will bring this hardware to life: exploring DEC's **RT-11**, **RSX-11**, and **RSTS/E** operating systems, how Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie used a PDP-11 to forge **Unix** and the **C language**, and how the PDP-11 shaped the **VAX**, **x86**, and modern computing!

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately traces how the PDP-11 evolved from the 1970 PDP-11/20 to the 1975 PDP-11/70 while keeping software compatible?
choices: Programs kept using 16-bit registers and orthogonal code while MMUs mapped virtual addresses across up to 4 MB
Every new PDP-11 model discarded the previous model's instruction set and required rewriting all software from scratch
The PDP-11/70 abandoned byte addressing and returned to the 12-bit single-accumulator design of the 1965 PDP-8
DEC replaced the UNIBUS and memory-mapped I/O with 80-column punch-card batch queues on all models after 1972
questions.explanation: The genius of the PDP-11 family was that user programs kept the exact same 16-bit `R0`–`R7` register model and orthogonal instruction set from the PDP-11/20 through the PDP-11/70, while hardware MMUs, split I/D spaces, and Kernel/User protection scaled physical memory up to 4 MB.

questions.prompt: Looking back across all ten sections of Part I, how do the PDP-11's major architectural pillars fit together during a single instruction like `MOVB (R1)+, @#177566` (copying a byte from a string to the Teletype printer)?
choices: It requires three separate special-purpose `IOT` instructions and a manual front-panel `DEP` switch flip for each letter
An orthogonal byte instruction reads via auto-increment `R1` and writes over the UNIBUS to a memory-mapped DBR
It halts the Processor Status Word, demagnetizes the RK05 disk platter, and waits overnight for an IBM batch operator
It converts the 16-bit Program Counter into a 12-bit accumulator and punches the character onto an 80-column card
questions.explanation: That single instruction showcases every pillar working in harmony: an orthogonal byte operation (`MOVB`), general-purpose register `R1` with auto-increment `(R1)+` stepping through byte-addressable memory, and a write across the asynchronous UNIBUS to the Teletype's memory-mapped Data Buffer Register (`177566`) in the upper I/O page.
